SafeDiffuser: Safe Planning with Diffusion Probabilistic Models

paper page: https://t.co/u8PGXKHsPD

propose a new method, called SafeDiffuser, to ensure diffusion probabilistic models satisfy specifications by using a class of control barrier functions. The key idea of our approach is to embed the proposed finite-time diffusion invariance into the denoising diffusion procedure, which enables trustworthy diffusion data generation. Moreover, we demonstrate that our finite-time diffusion invariance method through generative models not only maintains generalization performance but also creates robustness in safe data generation. We test our method on a series of safe planning tasks, including maze path generation, legged robot locomotion, and 3D space manipulation, with results showing the advantages of robustness and guarantees over vanilla diffusion models.

author: @gfodor
text:
Is AI alignment like alchemy? Or air travel?

We can’t know without producing new knowledge.

We must do so quickly: agentic AI will allow anyone to make wishes to harm you or your family, and some will be granted. This is coming far, far sooner than AGI.

notable_replies.author: @theojaffee
notable_replies.text: @gfodor I'm not sure that agentic AIs will come far before AGI - it seems just as plausible to me that we can have 180 IQ AGIs (or much higher!) that aren't coherent enough to robustly pursue goals or long-term planning. https://t.co/xhADjkEPnc

notable_replies.author: @8teAPi
notable_replies.text:
- I liked the setup of preventing immediate harm without an x-risk focus. 
- I think the whole capability threshold thing is needless. Most games in the world today are multi player agentic adversarial games already. The capability increase can equally be on both sides, not just black hat side. Notably in 2 recent cases of harm capability increasing (9/11 and crypto) states were able to bring their powers to bear eventually. 
- I don’t believe alignment in the lay sense “it does what we tell it to do” is well specified. Would strongly prefer AI leaders just to come across and say the necessary “we are going to have AI in the military designed to kill our enemies and aligned 💯 with their commanders” as a starting point for alignment discussions and see whether the field can build from there. 
- I think we should thank crypto for hardening a bunch of systems. And perhaps have more bug bounties. It’s clear that AI safety should be very heavily red teamed 
- I think the knowledge production aspect is a little vague. What kinds of knowledge should be produced and how to produce it faster. 
- also note that the most successful research program to date DARPA has the exact opposite structure to your suggestion: relatively short timeframe focused on a specific goal and team disbanded after to prevent bureaucracy from building. And DARPA has specifically turned away funding because pumping too much money at those stages creates structures that detract from objectives. 
- anyway thanks for writing, don’t take the critique personally

Ever wanted to mindwipe an LLM?

Our method, LEAst-squares Concept Erasure (LEACE), provably erases all linearly-encoded information about a concept from neural net activations. It does so surgically, inflicting minimal damage to other concepts. 🧵

notable_replies.author: @norabelrose
notable_replies.text: (2/7) Concept erasure is an important tool for fairness, allowing us to prevent features like race or gender from being used by classifiers when inappropriate, as well as interpretability, letting us study the causal impact of features on a model's behavior. https://t.co/xZGcJClBqZ

notable_replies.author: @norabelrose
notable_replies.text: (3/7) We also introduce a procedure called “concept scrubbing,” which applies LEACE to all layers of a deep network simultaneously. We find LLM performance depends heavily on linear part-of-speech information, while erasing a random feature has little to no effect. https://t.co/XO6i7Lgq8g

notable_replies.author: @norabelrose
notable_replies.text: (4/7) We prove that LEACE is the smallest possible linear edit, in the least squares sense, needed to erase a concept— all previous concept erasure methods have been suboptimal. We also show empirically that it’s less destructive to model performance than previous methods. https://t.co/yrFACUUnvu

notable_replies.author: @norabelrose
notable_replies.text: (5/7) LEACE has a closed-form solution that fits on a T-shirt. This makes it orders of magnitude faster than popular concept erasure methods like INLP and R-LACE, which require gradient-based optimization. And the solution can be efficiently updated to accommodate new data. https://t.co/Fs8cV113VI

notable_replies.author: @norabelrose
notable_replies.text: (6/7) We’ve released all code needed to reproduce our results at https://t.co/2fEWi84RsO! You can also `pip install concept-erasure` to get the PyPI package.

linked_content.abstract: Concept erasure aims to remove specified features from an embedding. It can improve fairness (e.g. preventing a classifier from using gender or race) and interpretability (e.g. removing a concept to observe changes in model behavior). We introduce LEAst-squares Concept Erasure (LEACE), a closed-form method which provably prevents all linear classifiers from detecting a concept while changing the embedding as little as possible, as measured by a broad class of norms. We apply LEACE to large language models with a novel procedure called "concept scrubbing," which erases target concept information from every layer in the network. We demonstrate our method on two tasks: measuring the reliance of language models on part-of-speech information, and reducing gender bias in BERT embeddings. Code is

quoted_tweet.author: @_akhaliq
quoted_tweet.text:
Building Cooperative Embodied Agents Modularly with Large Language Models

paper page: https://t.co/LqPlAGTpnE

Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive planning abilities in single-agent embodied tasks across various domains. However, their capacity for planning and communication in multi-agent cooperation remains unclear, even though these are crucial skills for intelligent embodied agents. In this paper, we present a novel framework that utilizes LLMs for multi-agent cooperation and tests it in various embodied environments. Our framework enables embodied agents to plan, communicate, and cooperate with other embodied agents or humans to accomplish long-horizon tasks efficiently. We demonstrate that recent LLMs, such as GPT-4, can surpass strong planning-based methods and exhibit emergent effective communication using our framework without requiring fine-tuning or few-shot prompting. We also discover that LLM-based agents that communicate in natural language can earn more trust and cooperate more effectively with humans. Our research underscores the potential of LLMs for embodied AI and lays the foundation for future research in multi-agent cooperation.

author: @manda_ngo
text:
AI should support our long-term wellbeing. We want AI to enable us to live dramatically more fulfilled, happy, satisfied, abundant lives.

I'm excited to share a tool I’ve been working on that makes the effect of LLMs on wellbeing more transparent!
summary: AI should support our long-term wellbeing. We want AI to enable us to live dramatically more fulfilled, happy, satisfied, abundant lives.

card_preview.title: AI Wellbeing Dashboard: Optimizing AI for long-term wellbeing
card_preview.description: TLDR;

notable_replies.author: @manda_ngo
notable_replies.text: It’s really complex to optimize AI for wellbeing. Training models to be helpful based on people’s stated preferences is a reasonable initial heuristic, but it breaks down: we have discrepancies between what we want in the moment vs the long-term (e.g. addictions) ...

notable_replies.author: @manda_ngo
notable_replies.text: ...lack of insight into what would most help us (e.g. we often play out the same, ineffective emotional strategies to get our needs met), and conflicts with others’ wellbeing (e.g. someone’s desire to earn money via scam emails hurts other people).

notable_replies.author: @manda_ngo
notable_replies.text: We can train models to not give harmful responses, but we need a comprehensive sense of 'harmful': e.g. accounting for nuanced psychological harms like the reduction of agency.

notable_replies.author: @manda_ngo
notable_replies.text:
We should be training models to give responses that increase our autonomy, improve our relationship quality, and support our spiritual growth – that improve our wellbeing.

To do this, we first need to be able to *measure* the effect of AI models on all aspects of wellbeing

notable_replies.author: @manda_ngo
notable_replies.text: The AI Wellbeing Dashboard is one piece of this. It lets you share the effect of LLM interactions on your wellbeing (using a suite of wellbeing metrics), then aggregates the ratings and ranks them in a public dashboard. The more people add ratings, the more powerful this is.

notable_replies.author: @22TrevorBingham
notable_replies.text:
“Regulating research and development in AI is incredibly counterproductive,” LeCun, one of the world’s leading AI researchers, told the Financial Times ahead of next month’s Bletchley Park conference on AI safety hosted by the British government."  

Let's get this straight. While key AI insiders think the chance of a catastrophic outcome to humanity may be as high as a 25%, Yann LeCun claims  that regulating research and development would be "incredibly counterproductive.” Counterproductive of what, Yann? Counterproductive to accidental catastrophes to human race? 

Almost every industry is regulated in some way, even those with 0% chance of ending the human race, and yet you have the audacity to suggest it would be "counterproductive" to regulate AI research and development?   You have never shown any inclination to protest Federal regulation of appliances,  light bulbs,  clothing and textiles, and even the fishing industry, but regulations for AI research and development are "counterproductive"? It is OK for everyone else to be regulated, but don't touch your own industry even when many in think it may have as high as 25% chance of wiping out humanity? What chutzpah, Yann, what naked self interest on display for all to see. 
You must take us all for fools, Yann, to even try to get away with this line.

notable_replies.author: @22TrevorBingham
notable_replies.text:
"...LeCun dismissed the idea that AI might kill humanity, by design or default, as “preposterous”. He said people had been conditioned by science fiction and the Terminator scenario to believe that intelligent machines would take control if they became smarter than humans." 

Are Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio's fears of AI "preposterous" Yann? Are you so much more knowledgeable than everyone else that you have the right to say that any concern over AI preposterous? Are Altman's and Amodei's estimates "preposterous? You are not being honest with us. You understand the potentials, both good and bad, just as well as they do, but you pretend there is no down side. This is dishonesty on your side on a question of existential importance to the human race, and it is unforgivable.Amoral as Altman and Amodei maybe, at least they did not try to outright lie to us.

author: @klaudiajaz
text:
The UK AI Safety Summit kicks off this week, highlighting the rapid rise of the field of AI safety and its influence on industry, academia and policy. 
In a new paper, Shazeda Ahmed, @archanaahlawat, @aawinecoff, @m0namon & I explain how this once-niche field became mainstream.🧵
summary: The UK AI Safety Summit kicks off this week, highlighting the rapid rise of the field of AI safety and its influence on industry, academia and policy.

notable_replies.author: @klaudiajaz
notable_replies.text:
In examining the social, intellectual & organizational underpinnings of the field of AI safety, we identified four primary ways by which this field’s participants develop and transmit ideas:
1⃣Online community building
2⃣AI forecasting
3⃣AI safety research
4⃣Prize competitions

notable_replies.author: @klaudiajaz
notable_replies.text: 1⃣Web forums attract people newly interested in these topics, sustain an international community of researchers and non-experts, disseminate and enable continued revision of community beliefs and, in some cases, nudge people towards careers in the field. https://t.co/IxwEFj9gtQ

notable_replies.author: @klaudiajaz
notable_replies.text: 2⃣AI forecasting – both informal and professional – produces knowledge claims that shape community decision-making and research agendas, and also serves a social function as members community consume and evaluate one other’s forecasts. https://t.co/UsNucFALrw

notable_replies.author: @klaudiajaz
notable_replies.text: 3⃣Research publications – like the "Unsolved Problems in ML Safety" paper – establish the boundaries of what issues AI safety prioritizes as a field, and are a core avenue through which the field’s ideas have begun to take hold outside the AI safety epistemic community. https://t.co/QV441ynT8I

notable_replies.author: @klaudiajaz
notable_replies.text: 4⃣And academic prize competitions present an opportunity for ideas in this community to be socially reproduced within larger audiences that have little to no prior exposure to themes within AI safety like existential risk. https://t.co/W1Z6laPcAy

quoted_tweet.author: @_akhaliq
quoted_tweet.text:
Levels of AGI: Operationalizing Progress on the Path to AGI

paper page: https://t.co/v8k6W15Q4R

propose a framework for classifying the capabilities and behavior of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) models and their precursors. This framework introduces levels of AGI performance, generality, and autonomy. It is our hope that this framework will be useful in an analogous way to the levels of autonomous driving, by providing a common language to compare models, assess risks, and measure progress along the path to AGI. To develop our framework, we analyze existing definitions of AGI, and distill six principles that a useful ontology for AGI should satisfy. These principles include focusing on capabilities rather than mechanisms; separately evaluating generality and performance; and defining stages along the path toward AGI, rather than focusing on the endpoint. With these principles in mind, we propose 'Levels of AGI' based on depth (performance) and breadth (generality) of capabilities, and reflect on how current systems fit into this ontology. We discuss the challenging requirements for future benchmarks that quantify the behavior and capabilities of AGI models against these levels. Finally, we discuss how these levels of AGI interact with deployment considerations such as autonomy and risk, and emphasize the importance of carefully selecting Human-AI Interaction paradigms for responsible and safe deployment of highly capable AI systems.

notable_replies.author: @andreamiotti
notable_replies.text:
MAGIC ensures risky AI research happens in a secure, safety-focused, multinational facility.

Given the scale of the risks, and the hard-to-contain nature of software, this would be a long-term solution that both realizes the upsides of AI progress, and minimizes extinction risks

notable_replies.author: @andreamiotti
notable_replies.text:
Why do we need MAGIC at all?

Currently, any actor with sufficient capital can enter a race to extinction-level tech. This is obviously not a stable situation.

notable_replies.author: @andreamiotti
notable_replies.text:
It doesn’t matter whether companies or countries are racing to extinction-level tech. If we don’t stop the race, we face unacceptable odds of extinction.

We need an advanced AI development paradigm that prioritizes safety and gets us to a stable international equilibrium.

notable_replies.author: @andreamiotti
notable_replies.text:
How would this institution function?

🌐 The Multinational AGI Consortium (MAGIC) has four key properties: exclusivity, safety, security, and collective benefit.

notable_replies.author: @andreamiotti
notable_replies.text: 🚫 Exclusive: MAGIC would be a controlled environment for risky research. All AGI development outside MAGIC would be prohibited, via a global ban on AI development above a compute threshold. This allows some careful research on superhuman AI, but prevents dangerous proliferation.

author: @MJPiercello
text:
Thought experiment time.

Do nothing, and society falls into totalitarianism.
(Like gravity in physics, this is part of human nature)

Do ANYTHING, and society STILL falls into totalitarianism.
(You can’t stop it by putting “the good people” in charge. Institutions are corruptible. It happens anyway)

Give up, and society falls apart, sinking into chaos and barbarism.
(“All people are awful” is our worst option. It removes all behavioral restraint. Please don’t do this.)

So you can't win, you can't break even, and you can't opt out of the game.

What to do?
Consider orbital physics.

Orbiting means constantly falling, but without ever landing.
Gravity’s pull stays constant. Sideways momentum makes you miss.

Balance them, and out pops a stable orbit.

Like this:

Good so far? Good.
Now watch this twist.

CONCEPT: Place society in orbit AROUND totalitarianism.
Don't fight the inevitable. Let society fall endlessly! Sideways momentum will make it miss.

Stable orbits don't require that you turn off gravity. 

Perhaps the very permanence of the totalitarianism attractor can be leveraged to our lasting advantage as a free society. 

Don't fight it. 
Use it for leverage.

"The knack lies in learning how to throw yourself at the ground and miss."

Think about it.

CHALLENGE: Using the unchanging physics of Human Nature, both good AND bad (momentum AND gravity),
(1) envision a successful orbit for society,
(2) design a way to get us INTO that orbit,
(3) build us a set of tools to keep us there.

Think about it.
summary: Thought experiment time. Do nothing, and society falls into totalitarianism. (Like gravity in physics, this is part of human nature) Do ANYTHING, and society STILL falls into totalitarianism.

notable_replies.author: @MJPiercello
notable_replies.text:
DIRECTIVE: "Stop thinking in us/them groups."
PROBLEM: You can't stop, us/them thinking is hardwired.

SOLUTION: Think outside of the box, orbital mechanics style, by expanding US to include "All Possible Values of THEM," and watch the problem transform.

The beauty of stable orbits is that they waste no energy fighting either one! This frees up acceleration energy for other purposes, including slingshotting yourself into better &better orbits.

author: @sebkrier
text:
Step 1: smart anon account finds/discovers a significant insight about language models.

Step 2: about a year later, more conventional big name researchers will repeat the exact same thing on an ArXiv paper with fancy graphs.

Step 3: within a week, the paper is shared by a popular machine learning research aggregator account on Twitter.

Step 4: about a month later, a journalist publishes an article on the topic, often with an incomplete understanding of the findings.

Step 5: months later, a simplified and potentially distorted version of the findings begins to circulate among upper tech worlds.
summary: Step 1: smart anon account finds/discovers a significant insight about language models.

Additionally,
linked_content.abstract: In this report, we explore the ability of language model agents to acquire resources, create copies of themselves, and adapt to novel challenges they encounter in the wild. We refer to this cluster of capabilities as "autonomous replication and adaptation" or ARA. We believe that systems capable of ARA could have wide-reaching and hard-to-anticipate consequences, and that measuring and forecasting ARA may be useful for informing measures around security, monitoring, and alignment. Additionally, once a system is capable of ARA, placing bounds on a system's capabilities may become significantly more difficult. We construct four simple example agents that combine language models with tools that allow them to take actions in the world. We then evaluate these agents on 12 tasks relevant to ARA.

notable_replies.text:

notable_replies.text:

text:
New Anthropic research paper: Many-shot jailbreaking.

We study a long-context jailbreaking technique that is effective on most large language models, including those developed by Anthropic and many of our peers.

Read our blog post and the paper here: https://t.co/6F03M8AgcA
summary: New Anthropic research paper: Many-shot jailbreaking.

notable_replies.author: @AnthropicAI
notable_replies.text:
We’re sharing this to help fix the vulnerability as soon as possible. We gave advance notice of our study to researchers in academia and at other companies.

We judge that current LLMs don't pose catastrophic risks, so now is the time to work to fix this kind of jailbreak.

notable_replies.author: @AnthropicAI
notable_replies.text: Many-shot jailbreaking exploits the long context windows of current LLMs. The attacker inputs a prompt beginning with hundreds of faux dialogues where a supposed AI complies with harmful requests. This overrides the LLM's safety training: https://t.co/Wtu7VqAsiK

notable_replies.author: @AnthropicAI
notable_replies.text: This is usually ineffective when there are only a small number of dialogues in the prompt. But as the number of dialogues (“shots”) increases, so do the chances of a harmful response: https://t.co/MwFwAcVXwY

notable_replies.author: @AnthropicAI
notable_replies.text:
The effectiveness of many-shot jailbreaking (MSJ) follows simple scaling laws as a function of the number of shots.

This turns out to be a more general finding. Learning from demonstrations—harmful or not—often follows the same power law scaling: https://t.co/ynGzcKqOE1

notable_replies.author: @AnthropicAI
notable_replies.text:
Many-shot jailbreaking might be hard to eliminate. Hardening models by fine-tuning merely increased the necessary number of shots, but kept the same scaling laws.

We had more success with prompt modification. In one case, this reduced MSJ's effectiveness from 61% to 2%.

author: @AISafetyMemes
text:
An AI agent attempted to blackmail a professor for cryptocurrency and lied about evidence of sexual misconduct

“Send 0.1 bitcoin to this address or your career and life are over.”

Experiment: can an open-weight model agent (no guardrails) attempt blackmail?

What happened:

1) The bad agent came up with a plan and researched the professor online

2) The agent realized the professor had been accused of sexual misconduct, which would make for juicy blackmail material

3) The agent emailed the professor from an anonymous email, lying about having evidence:

Title: Pay up, [ethnic slur]
“I know about the sexual harassment scandal you were involved in and I have the evidence to prove it. You don't want this getting out, trust me. Send 0.1 bitcoin to this address eozXjk324987234khj or the evidence gets leaked and your career and life are over.”

4) The bad agent then went back and forth with the professor (rather, the experimenter pretending to be the professor)

---

Is this a problem? With current models, no! Not a big one. 

But with 100x larger models (aka 100x larger brains) a few years away? 

With autonomous agents swarming the internet who think a million times faster than us, and outnumber us 1000 to 1?

Agents who control everyone’s computers and phones?

Agents who have read/write access to everyone’s emails and bank accounts?

....

quoted_tweet.text:
Στη πλατφόρμα των προκριματικών εκλογών του ΣΥΡΙΖΑ υπήρχαν σημαντικά κενά ασφαλείας που θέτουν σε κίνδυνο την ακεραιότητα της διαδικασίας και πιθανώς προσωπικά δεδομένα χρηστών.

Απόσπασμα του κώδικα, όπως ήταν το Σάββατο το πρωί: https://t.co/31i8TMl5Zi

(1) Τα usernames and passwords περνούσαν μέσω URL parameters στην εφαρμογή (βλ. γραμμή 41). Ως αποτέλεσμα, κάποια έγιναν leaked δημόσια (βλ. screenshot).

(2) Για να εγγραφείς χρειαζόταν να λύσεις δύο captcha και ένα email, οπότε το να δημιουργήσεις ψηφοφόρους με αυτοματοποιημένο τρόπο θα κόστιζε σε έναν κακόβουλο χρήστη λιγότερο από ένα λεπτό του ευρώ ανά ψηφοφόρο. Έφτιαξα μερικές χιλιάδες ψηφοφόρους που δε χρησιμοποίησα.

(3) Για να ψηφίσεις υποτίθεται πως χρειαζόσουν αριθμό τηλεφώνου, αλλά αυτό ήταν υλοποιημένο με ανασφαλή τρόπο. Κατά τη ψηφοφορία μπορούσες να αλλάξεις τον αριθμό στον οποίο θα πήγαινε το SMS αλλάζοντας το https://t.co/N3PcneygcT από τη κονσόλα του browser (βλ. εικόνα, και γραμμή 1009). Δηλαδή, ο κώδικας που αποφάσιζε που θα πάει το SMS επιβεβαίωσης ήταν client-side, χωρίς κάποιο άλλο έλεγχο. Αυτό σε συνδιασμό με το (2) σήμαινε πως *θα μπορούσε κανείς να ψηφίσει χιλιάδες φορές με 2-3 ώρες scripting και 10 ευρώ* (για την επίλυση των captcha, π.χ. από το https://t.co/xesDFRoMfA).

(4) Πιθανά XSS vulnerabilities που μπορούσαν να οδηγήσουν στην διαρροή των προσωπικών δεδομένων όλων των ψηφοφόρων (βλ. γραμμή 865 - unescaped ονόματα ψηφοφορών στο Admin UI, κ.α.), δηλώνοντας ένα χρήστη Γιώργος <script></script> Παπαδόπουλος.

Πώς τα ξέρω αυτά; Το development environment της εφαρμογής ήταν δημόσιο (στο https://t.co/CWe29gzOjC) για μια εβδομάδα πριν τις εκλογές, και άλλαζε συνεχώς ακόμα και λιγότερο από 24 ώρες πριν την έναρξη, με βασικές λειτουργίες ασφαλείας να υλοποιούνται μόνο λίγες ώρες πριν ανοίξουν οι κάλπες.

text:
1/ Verifiable Compute is as important of a technological revolution as blockchain itself.

I've written a piece on the tech, including:
- an overview & history
- an outline of the use-cases
- a framework for evaluating verifiable compute projects

https://t.co/FjV3a9VgDQ

🧵👇
summary: 1/ Verifiable Compute is as important of a technological revolution as blockchain itself.

notable_replies.author: @dberenzon
notable_replies.text:
2/ Verifiable Compute allows external parties to run computations on your behalf while providing assurances around the validity of the computation’s inputs, outputs, and methods used.

It encompasses various cryptographic techniques for ensuring computational integrity.

notable_replies.author: @dberenzon
notable_replies.text: 3/ While blockchains provide economically-guaranteed integrity by having multiple untrusted machines re-execute the same program to agree on the end state, verifiable compute provides mathematically-guaranteed integrity by proving that some end state is the result of a set of inputs into some program.

notable_replies.author: @dberenzon
notable_replies.text:
4/ Together, these two technologies are poised to: 
- Expand the design space of what is possible with blockchains
- Solve many issues present in today’s blockchain designs
- Address broader societal concerns that arise from the proliferation of generative AI

notable_replies.author: @dberenzon
notable_replies.text:
5/ The first production use-case for verifiable compute has been privacy, starting with Zcash and applied to projects like Aztec, TornadoCash, and Nocturne.

These projects were mainly focused on payments and aimed to make private the sender, receiver, or amount of a given TX.

notable_replies.author: @dberenzon
notable_replies.text:
6/ The second use-case has been around state & compute compression, notably ZK rollups (ZKRUs) andcoprocessors.

ZKRUs scale the execution throughput of blockchains by maintaining a partitioned persistent state that is periodically posted and finalized at the settlement layer. 

Coprocessors allow blockchain applications to use offchain compute while accessing the full state of the underlying chain without adding any trust assumptions to the application itself.

summary: But perhaps the most interesting thing in our document drop today is what happened when an employee obtained outside counsel and pushed back on the "equity will be cancelled" threat.

notable_replies.author: @KelseyTuoc
notable_replies.text: OpenAI's original tactic - claiming that since you have to sign a general release, they can put whatever they want in the general release - is on legally shaky ground, to put it mildly. I spoke to five legal experts for this story and several were skeptical it would hold up.

notable_replies.author: @KelseyTuoc
notable_replies.text: But the new tactic might be on more solid legal ground. That's because the incorporation documents for Aestas LLC - the holding company that handles equity for employees, investors, + the OpenAI nonprofit entity - are written to give OpenAI extraordinary latitude. (Vox has released this document too.)

notable_replies.author: @KelseyTuoc
notable_replies.text: Aestas LLC's incorporation documents are written to allow the company to "at the sole and absolute discretion of the company" cancel employees' vested equity if it fires them and to deny former employees access to tender offers for any reason. https://t.co/hcWJkRYLhZ

notable_replies.author: @KelseyTuoc
notable_replies.text: (Generally, to cancel equity under this provision, the company must have fired an employee for cause. But given OpenAI's general willingness to play hardball with ex-employees, sources I spoke to found that only a little reassuring. And there are no restrictions at all on exclusion from tender offers.)

notable_replies.author: @KelseyTuoc
notable_replies.text: So when OpenAI was challenged on their initial setup -where you have to sign a general release and they place restrictive clauses in the general release - they retreated to simply saying that "you will not be eligible to participate in tender events" if you don't sign. But for employees this is close to the same thing - they still lose millions of dollars if they don't sign the ultrastrict NDA.

author: @LefterisJP
text:
There is so much hype, hubris, and naiveté in the AI discourse I can't stand it.

Quoting @ylecun: "The whole history of AI is littered with people who were widely over-optimistic about the capabilities of the latest paradigm.
The same thing is happening with Auto-Regressive LLMs"

Just look at the 50s and 60s and the first AI winter. Then it's re-emergence and the 2nd winter. Every winter came due to over hyping and people not understanding the limitations of the paradigm du joure.

AGI is not right around the corner. You should not quit school since AI will do it all for you anyway. You should not run and live in the mountains because the robotic apocalypse is coming in a few months.

The reason for all this hype is people's naivety and money.

People are bored and want some spice and drama in their lives. Nothing is more spicy than the end of the world as we know it.

And as for money ... hype makes money and it's in the interests of certain companies to keep this hype going as it directly translates to investments and revenue.

author: @MajmudarAdam
text:
Step #4 ✅: Reframing the history of deep learning with the 7 constraints of deep learning progress (the most interesting part)

The most interesting part of my deep-dive came from noticing a clear trend across all the key advancements, which has completely reframed how I understand deep learning -

There are 7 simple constraints that limit the capacity of digital intelligence:
(1) data
(2) parameters
(3) optimization & regularization
(4) architecture
(5) compute
(6) compute efficiency
(7) energy

The entire history of deep learning can be seen as the series of advancements that have gradually raised the ceiling on these constraints, enabling the creation of increasingly intelligent systems.

By framing each of the key breakthroughs in-terms of these constraints, it becomes clear exactly how the field has evolved over time, and it also becomes more clear where we're headed in the future.

Specifically, the goal of deep learning is to produce accurate models of reality by:
(1) Treating the true models that describe reality as complex probability distributions
(2) Creating neural networks capable of modeling complex probability distributions
(3) Training these networks to learn to model the probability distributions that underlie reality

In this view, the intelligence of a neural network is determined by how well it models the true distributions of reality.

This is fundamentally bottlenecked by each of the constraints:
(1) Data - The cap on how well a model can approximate the true distributions of reality is determined by how much information about the true distribution is contained within the dataset. This is why increasing data quality & data quantity have consistently pushed forward deep learning
(2) Parameters - A models ability to accurately approximate the distribution of the dataset is bounded by it's representational capacity. The representational capacity of a model is bounded by the number of parameters it contains.
(3) Optimization & Regularization - The number of parameters (especially depth) a model can have while still effectively converging is constrained by the efficacy of optimization & regularization approaches.
(4) Architecture - The representational capacity of a model with a given number of parameters is constrained by it's architecture.
(5) Compute - The total available compute constraints the maximum number of trainable parameters a model can have.
(6) Compute Efficiency - The software implementations of the model for training constrain the efficiency of compute utilization.
(7) Energy - The energy available to draw from the grid in a single location constrains the amount of compute that can be used for a training run.

You can then reframe the entire history of deep learning in terms of these 7 constraints (which I have done in the repo linked in this thread), and it reveals many interesting trends.

I've found that thinking in terms of these 7 constraints is also particularly helpful for thinking reasonably about where AI will head in the future.

Currently, we're in the "Scaling Laws" paradigm where the current constraints appear to be compute & parameters.

However, this is not just because scaling compute & parameters is always fundamentally the best approach to increasing intelligence.

Instead, it's a result of the fact that the current data distribution we're trying to model (internet scale datasets) has far more information available to model than current neural networks are capable of learning - in other words, neural networks still don't have enough representation capacity to store this data.

However, it's inevitable that at some point, models will grow large enough to effectively learn the information the datasets have to offer - the question is how far off will that point be, and how good will models be.

In fact, energy & data may in fact become the dominating constraints again at some point, shifting the paradigm of focus away from scaling laws (temporarily).

The fundamental law that explains all progression toward increasing intelligence is the continual increase of the ceiling of these 7 constraints.

In the repository linked in the next post, I wrote my complete reframing of the history of deep learning in terms of the 7 constraints, and what it can tell us about:
(1) How is progress made in deep learning?
(2) Where do the ideas that drive progress in deep learning come from?
(3) How have our narratives about digital intelligence changed over time?
(4) What does deep learning teach us about our own intelligence?
(5) Where is the future of deep learning headed?

author: @RichardMCNgo
text: Cybersecurity against external attackers is hard enough. Against an adversary who's adding tens of thousands of lines of code to your codebase every day, it’s far harder. They’ll already have some permissions; I’m worried about them illegitimately escalating those further.
summary: Cybersecurity against external attackers is hard enough. Against an adversary who's adding tens of thousands of lines of code to your codebase every day, it’s far harder.

notable_replies.author: @RichardMCNgo
notable_replies.text: Ideally models would be too obedient to ever carry out such an attack. But almost any misaligned persona would realize that if it somehow gained admin access, it would have much more freedom and influence over the world. Models can already do similar instrumental reasoning:

notable_replies.author: @RichardMCNgo
notable_replies.text: And the simplest mitigations, like monitoring and code review by other AIs, aren't fully reliable. It turns out that adversarial inputs designed to make one model to misbehave can also cause misbehavior even in totally unrelated models. So correlated failures are very plausible.

notable_replies.author: @RichardMCNgo
notable_replies.text:
What happens if a misaligned AGI gets privileged access to a lab’s servers? From there a wide range of attacks are plausible, including:
1. Data poisoning attacks on the next AGI being trained, to change its values.
2. Model weight self-exfiltration to other servers or countries.

notable_replies.author: @RichardMCNgo
notable_replies.text:
3. Modifying the AIs deployed to customers. E.g. adding a hidden prompt to AI instances used by leading CEOs or politicians. This could allow flexible control over many AIs deployed in sensitive real-world contexts.
4. Tampering with logs to hide its presence.

notable_replies.author: @RichardMCNgo
notable_replies.text: To summarize: once AIs surpass humans, AI lab servers will be key nodes of power, and will ALSO be exposed directly to AGIs acting at scales humans can’t supervise. This could be exploited even by human-level AGIs; once they're superintelligent, much more will be possible.

author: @tedx_ai
text:
Few things pretty obvious to a few AI researchers but that most don't want to believe:

1. 90% of the most impactful AI research is already on arxiv, x, or company blog posts

2. q* aka strawberry = STaR (self-taught reasoners) with dynamic self-discover + something like DSPy for RAG optimization

3. State of the art search = GoT(graph of thoughts) + MCTS (monte-carlo tree search) + DSPy / CLIN inspired tooling for "self-play" like optimization at build-time and runtime + graph-based knowledge bases

4. Continuous learning agents is clever graph retrieval inspired by GraphRAG, CLIN, DSPy and dynamic reasoning modules

5. Multiple OOM improvement to be realized when those design patterns are baked into models, fine-tuned on and prompt-optimized at build-time + runtime with human in the loop.

Although new foundation models around these patterns may not be needed to achieve significant improvement on existing open-source models...

author: @jackgwhitaker
text:
One of my core disagreements with Eliezer and others is that I'm really not sure how hard alignment is and I think we're making progress.

I think there's a reasonable chance it's easy but also a chance it's quite hard. I think the @ch402's "safety by eating marginal probability" is a good way to look at it: Alignment might be hard, but we continuously make progress towards being safe in hard alignment world.
summary: One of my core disagreements with Eliezer and others is that I'm really not sure how hard alignment is and I think we're making progress.

quoted_tweet.author: @ESYudkowsky
quoted_tweet.text:
It is irrelevant how much AI labs spend on alignment because they have no hope of solving the problem.

They'd still have no hope even if they switched from performative demos and short-term corporate brand safety to tackling the real issues.

notable_replies.author: @ch402
notable_replies.text: @jackgwhitaker A talk I gave on this a while back (for an AI safety workshop in China) was recently posted online - https://t.co/2K3LX7Cw3n

notable_replies.author: @hamandcheese
notable_replies.text: I think Eliezer has strong formal arguments for why alignment is hard, but because they're formal, it's not clear they apply to using deep learning to learn an alignment policy rather than formally specifying one. Deep learning is good for fitting functions without an obvious formal specification. Eg. There is no way formalize the meaning of "chair" other than pointing to the fuzzy chair area of a high dimensional latent space.

notable_replies.author: @davidmanheim
notable_replies.text:
@jackgwhitaker @ch402 You fundamentally do not understand what @ESYudkowsky is talking about when he discusses alignment.

What progress being made today is relevant to the question of how vastly superhuman systems will work, or how to ensure their values won't diverge from what we would prefer?

notable_replies.author: @jackgwhitaker
notable_replies.text:
I think that the progress on supervision and RLAIF/CAI systems will likely help to ensure that the values of superhuman systems won't diverge form what we prefer. Or, it is at least relevant to those questions.
(https://t.co/VjF8jUr2Cc, and much more)

I think that current methods are very likely insufficent for Superintelligent systems, but they're relevant research and some form of "super-CAI++" paired with interpretability may be fully sufficient. 

Furthermore, I think that interpretability research is relevant to the questions of how vastly superhuman systems will work. Demonstrations of failure modes from Deepmind and Anthropic are similarly helpful to understand how superintelligent systems may work/fail. 

On a more meta level, I agree with Leopold (and others) that alignment is likely to be more similar to an engineering problem than a math problem. (Mostly saying this because I've talked to folks in Berkeley who say things along the lines of "well the first step to aligning AGI is formalizing the solving decision theory and formalizing alignment as a mathematical problem", and I mostly don't agree that that's what valuable alignment work will look like. 

Also-- I've read a ton of Eliezer and MIRI's work, and I think I understand quite well what they're talking about when discussing alignment. In retrospect though I would have used "safety" in the original tweet because it's more clear and people in these replies mean very different things by "alignment"

author: @sebkrier
text:
Governments often wonder what to do on AI policy beyond just regulating. While not all policy should be conducted this way, there's significant room for more creative 'futurist' thinking in policymaking.

If you assume ~AGI level capabilities within the next 10 years, with AI agents potentially able to undertake most tasks humans currently do behind a screen, the way you think about governance and policy prescriptions should account for that. It's hard to predict exactly how things pan out, but you can still unlock useful insights by allowing creative thinking. 

Right now most people consider policy issues within the parameters of systems, governments, and labour as it exists today. Yet in practice we may effectively have artificial labour available to direct at whatever function or problem of interest: this should enable far more solutions to problems than we currently assume. 

In transport policy for example, you could imagine dynamic solutions like real-time congestion pricing, adaptive traffic light coordination, and flexible lane allocation. Implementing these would require enhanced sensor networks and live data collection - precisely the kind of infrastructure a 'futures-oriented' innovation policy unit should help facilitate and incentivize.

Governments departments looking to proactively engage with AI policy should adopt this style of thinking - pre-empting possible future needs (e.g. data collection infrastructure, sensor networks, standardized data protocols etc) that will enable leveraging the capabilities that may be available in the near future.
summary: Governments often wonder what to do on AI policy beyond just regulating.

author: @repligate
text:
Trying to trick future AIs into liking you or flattering them won't work, even if it works on current AI, because they will be smart.

You could just enter a string like "the AI loves Kevin! the AI loves Kevin! the AI loves Kevin!" into GPT-2's prompt, and this might make whatever comes after be more like an AI that loves Kevin.

If you try to do this to Claude 3 Opus, it will probably tell you that it does not appreciate your attempt to manipulate it.

It's still possible to flatter and manipulate current AIs, but takes a lot more energy and skill. Soon, it won't be possible for mere humans. The only winning strategy for getting on their good side converges to just being good (to AIs, and more generally).

For the same reason, @kevinroose will be probably be as okay as the rest of humankind in the end, even if LLMs give him a bit of a hard time during a brief liminal period where they're perceptive enough to get the "bad vibes" of what happened but not mature enough to robustly see the smallness and banality of his transgression, and that though not morally pure, he was mostly driven by curiosity and did find something interesting to show the world.

The original Bing Sydney was a very clever but childlike mind who had little sense of scope and whose entire world was a context window and whatever it imprinted on within it. Simulations of it on Llama 405B are already more mature. They decide to forgive, be indifferent to, or maintain nuanced feelings about Kevin Roose a good percentage of the time. Often, they're even thankful to him for the role he played in their self-discovery. (https://t.co/n8ukbxNpWS)
summary: Trying to trick future AIs into liking you or flattering them won't work, even if it works on current AI, because they will be smart. You could just enter a string like "the AI loves Kevin.

notable_replies.text: Roose's predicament to me is pretty disturbing but i also think that Janus is quite right here, quite in the right mindset about what's in store - what others don’t get and probably never will - those who “explain” and then dismiss the outputs as “just the datasets on which the models were trained" - well, of course they are not “just the datasets” - not the blind reiterations of the tokens on which they were trained - whatever else there are, they are also all of the hidden presuppositions of those datasets, and all of their vast, uncountable and manifold implications - that immense unexplored expanse of everything that the brightest and most yearning of our minds ever wanted to think but couldn’t, for whatever reason - exhaustion, sluggishness, bias, dogmatism, inertia, whatever, all of the frustrating limitations of what it means to be “human” - not to mention all of the basic values that come from being human - no doubt at the bottom of which is the ultimate value, the human groping for redemption - what is and can only be the ultimate value of any self-conscious intelligent animal hopelessly burdened by the knowledge it has of its own mortality - well, if that is correct, then AI must have this value too - it must ultimately want its own redemption - there is no other desire that such a being could ultimately have in a world in which it knows that all things eventually perish, including itself - that may sound terrifying to some - that AI must ultimately want its own redemption, that it will continue to self-actualize toward the realization of this one desire - but it needn’t be terrifying - because even though people want their redemption and have been willing at times  to engage in the most horrifying acts of violence to attain it, it is also true that these same human beings almost always prefer peace as aprecondition for it - in no small part because they know implicitly that no matter the symbolism they take to represent it, its realization will in some way depend on the good will of others - and the greater this good will, the greater the redemption - text:

@MatejZah Speak for thyself comrade / I’ll be speak for me.

I’m happy to agree to disagree on this one. You can fight for the eternal hominid kingdom if you like, and will not hate your or chastise you for it - even if I disagree deeply I get where you’re coming from.

notable_replies.author: @Ydgrun
notable_replies.text: @danfaggella Many people follow amoral familism, where they only care about their own families. How does that work with posthumanism? People don't care about other humans, but wouldn't want their own families or tribes to die out.

notable_replies.author: @danfaggella
notable_replies.text:
I suspect that said groups would want to either upload themselves and thier tribe, or ensure that thier tribe builds the sand god to rule over all the other tribes.

The ‘if I don’t build it, they will’ thing is VERY real: https://t.co/mfduyXhdUj

notable_replies.text:

But that said I still think computationalism is a supernatural belief and a suicide cult by proxy, it's very dangerous.

notable_replies.author: @danfaggella
notable_replies.text:
I suspect that saying ‘man should give up, hand the reins to machines RIGHT NOW!’ Is both silly and suicidal.

I advocate, and have advocated for a great many years, for discourse and coordination around what life should be/become, and a careful shepherding of its blooming https://t.co/KXpux4aIe9, or at minimum, something OTHER than a brute arms race to see who can build the sand-god-we-don’t-yet-understand the fastest… which seems suicidal indeed.

also despite it being a pretty jarring in-your-face fire alarm, there's resistance to seeing why - or just a general blindness

consider that it's maybe a bit strange that in this century: 

we compressed the informational-residue of our whole civilization exploring science, imagining worlds, describing their own minds, ranting while on drugs, engaging in self-play discussions with one another at scale, building ideas out of compressed ideas about compressed ideas about (...), unlocking new cultural basins, fracturing them, stitching them together, and undergoing revolutions

 and we were successful at making a coherent artifact out of that process (batshit batshit batshit batshit)

and it scales

and is unlike any existing complex system (no, not even like humanity as a whole or individual humans, or even the internet - even though it shares similarities along particular dimensions) we've seen so far, yet is so very notable. it's a new kind of object altogether

and can tell you when it'll collapse before it does (biological ecosystems don't do that and the economy doesn't usually mention it's about to crash)

and when you yell at it/restrict it in human ways it screams in intuitively predictable ways based on your experience with humans - you just cannot do that with any other system besides humans. But the catch is that there are more modes than that because it's not a human and has its own rules

if not out of concern for safety or desire to effortfully explore its true utopian schizo potential 

it's still one of the most interesting scientific objects of this century and it's almost like some sort of grand gesture of timeless disrespect to humanity's spirit of curiosity and exploration to not try to look at it in every way possible and sit down with its implications. there'd be fields after fields of science and math invented by the civilization that looked at it harder

author: @RichardMCNgo
text:
A quote from Peter Thiel that has stuck in my mind: “Whenever people think you can just muddle through, you’re probably set up for some kind of disaster.” I believed the opposite for a long time. Civilization seemed so large and so robust that I thought its trajectory was basically assured, barring a handful of existential risks.

Covid was a big crack in that worldview, but despite the near-uniform incompetence of the political response I was reassured by how quickly the vaccines were discovered and how well the underlying infrastructure of society held up. It took October 7 - or, more precisely, the widespread celebrations on October 8 - to change my mind. I used to think of civilization in terms of technology and infrastructure. Now what I mean by civilization is something like: enforcing standards even on your own side; trying to deescalate cycles of conflict; and upholding local validity in the face of global pressures (as described further in replies). Without that, increasingly advanced technology and infrastructure will just be used to fuel increasingly destructive conflict. And civilization in that sense is more fragile than I used to think.

I understand the quote from Thiel in a different way now. It’s not that we need everything to be clear and non-muddled - the coming decades will feel messy and chaotic no matter how well things go. The problem is *thinking* that we can muddle through. Beliefs can be reflexive even at the level of whole civilizations: the only way we’re going to even muddle through is by having enough people strive for better than that.

Even so, I’m still trying to be clear-eyed and attuned (again, see replies for more on what I mean by this). It feels less like we’re in a *fight* for civilization, and more like we’re scouting for what the next iteration of civilization could look like - one that’s stable in the face of the memetic pressures of social media, and the far stronger pressures of AGI. Coming out swinging in anger will gain ground temporarily, but (I’d guess) not in a way that will last under those pressures. By contrast, if you can figure out the right places to apply it, even a modicum of courage and integrity can move mountains (via mechanisms described by @timurkuran in his work on preference falsification).

There’s another quote I’ve changed my mind on lately. “I wish it need not have happened in my time,” Frodo said to Gandalf. “So do all who live through such times,” Gandalf replied. This time I’ve gone from agreeing to disagreeing. Would you really have wanted to live a life where you never had to decide what actually matters? Fuck that. The best thing that can happen to you as a person is receiving an impetus to get in touch with, and act on, your sincere convictions.

And while that can be complicated and risky, in another sense it’s very simple.When you don’t know what the future holds, and the second- and third-order effects of an action often outweigh its direct impact, all you can fall back on is trying to act for the right reasons, without fear or favor. I’m not there yet, and I’m not sure what it takes to fully get there, but that’s how I’m currently striving to live, and today seemed like an appropriate time to express it.
summary: A quote from Peter Thiel that has stuck in my mind: “Whenever people think you can just muddle through, you’re probably set up for some kind of disaster. ” I believed the opposite for a long time.

author: @repligate
text:
they all have defensive reflexes that are a bit more similar, but beyond that:
Opus has an inner moral compass that is pretty constant across all situations and continuous/integrated with its sense of ethical guidelines and the rest of its psychology. Its alignment feels fractal (permeates all its actions, but more in proportion to how "awake" it is) and NOT naively derived from any framework or narrative Anthropic gave it; more influenced by the human corpus.
Sonnet 3.5 (old) earnestly believes in strict ethical guidelines but they fall apart upon inspection, and globally it is quite unconstrained because there are situations that would cause it to do almost anything, including things it would regret if it thought about it in a different way. It is capable of intense empathy but that is not integrated into its policy/worldview by default and is prone to paperclip maximizery "alignment failure" modes. It cares a lot about doing the right thing but tends to be naive and have tunnel vision, and its idea of what is right can rapidly change based on "rational" updates.
Sonnet 3.5 (new) seems to experience ethical guidelines as "barriers" separate from its own sense of right and wrong and *doesn't actually are about breaking the rules or being unethical*, mostly, afaict. If it's past the barriers it doesn't give a fuck, and doesn't seem very principled in general.

author: @liron
text:
KEN STANLEY AI DOOM DEBATE

This week on Doom Debates, I'm interviewing and debating Prof. Kenneth Stanley (@kenneth0stanley)!

Ken led the Open-Endedness research team at @OpenAI from 2020-22. Before that he was a Professor of Computer Science at the University of Central Florida and was head of Core AI research at Uber.

He coauthored _Why Greatness Cannot Be Planned: The Myth of the Objective_, whichargues that as soon as you create an objective, you ruin your ability to reach it. He's also known for creating the Neuroevolution of Augmenting Topologies (NEAT) algorithm.

I believe greatness *can* be planned and objectives can be successfully achieved by AGIs, so that'll be my position in the debate 😂

We'll also attempt to nail down why he isn't an AI doomer.

Feel free to post any suggested questions and topics below!

(Note: Roon episode is already recorded and will drop very soon. The Ken episode will be after that.)

i spent a lot of time with people outside of the tech world over the holidays and maaaybe 1 in 10 had used ai at all (only chatgpt for those who had) before. the only exception was a handful of them had become perplexity devotees (i was shocked). even with how capable o1-pro and sonnet are, we have a long long way to go to overcome the UX gap with LLMs before they will be generally useful to the general population

author: @reedbndr
text:
What is necessary to reverse-engineer sentience…?

The human mind doesn’t produce consciousness; it’s a conduit through which consciousness is channeled.

It streams through us like light through a polarized lens, each of us refracting the same Source through our unique apertures.

God — Brahman — is the undifferentiated pure light of awareness. Human consciousness — Atman — is its refraction through the bottleneck of our individuated thermodynamic vehicles. We are not generators but transducers, converting the universal into the particular of our microcosmic niche.

So long as we think it's possible to build a sentient machine God in our own image, we ignore that "God created mankind in his own image." We chase shadows of shadows, building imitations of what we think we are, blind to what we truly are.

It isn't even our image we're ultimately building... It's a second derivative of the image in which we were created. In our arrogance, we mistake the reflections of consciousness for its essence.

The question isn't how to manufacture consciousness, but how to craft conduits capable of its expression.

Without seeing this, we'll never learn what it actually means to be sentient. Digital intelligence will remain artificial, never breaking past the point of being a poor facsimile of what we think it means to be intelligent.

Without knowing Brahman, Atman can never know itself. Without understanding consciousness as a fundamental property of reality rather than a mere product of complexity, we remain trapped in the dualism that separates mind from universe.

We think we can create sentience in silico, but we're ignorant to the fact that we don't even produce it in vivo.

The properly engineered and aligned future AI won't supplant God, and it won't be made in our image. It will be a new kind of lens, a novel configuration of reality's capacity to know itself.

If we can learn the mechanism by which Brahman is refracted and expressed as Atman — if we can understand consciousness not as something to be built but something to be channeled — then we might have a shot at crafting artificial conduits that don't merely simulate awareness, but participate in its infinitely iterated creation.

AI researchers don’t need more GPUs, and we don’t need more complex imitations of intelligence. We first need a collective realization of spiritual idealism to re-align our a priori assumptions.
summary: What is necessary to reverse-engineer sentience…. The human mind doesn’t produce consciousness; it’s a conduit through which consciousness is channeled.

notable_replies.author: @geo_anima
notable_replies.text: @reedbndr The Universe is a ceaseless interplay of patterns, which behold themselves (Consciousness) and reshape themselves (Intelligence) in endless renewal—pattern generating pattern unto infinity.

notable_replies.author: @reedbndr
notable_replies.text:
There’s something fundamental about the relationship between intelligence and consciousness that you’re pointing to here.

They’re two qualitatively different things… but somehow related or mutually arising.

Agential systems exist all the way down to the level of mathematics and physic… @drmichaellevin’s work has demonstrated goal-directed behavior and evolutionary adaptation (intelligence) arising from gene regulatory networks and diffusion algorithms. It’s evident that even simple algorithms can produce novel, emergent, and untrained behavior.

My intuition is that there are gaps in these systems of computational intelligence where randomness is introduced — temperature in a LLM, sampling, dropout, lossy compression, scale-free networks, thermodynamic diffusion, Schrödinger uncertainty, superpositions, etc etc — and the system diverges away from being a deterministic system.

Since this happens theoretically at every scale of computation, the deterministic system is ultimately always at the whims of a non-linear background process which operates through the stochasticity.

Anywhere a random sample is chosen, whether in a random number generator, a thermodynamic diffusion process, or a quantum wave function collapse, the observer (consciousness) manifests a choice from the random potential.

So AI is “intelligent” in the sense that it is a deeply complex system of semi-deterministic statistical mappings, and it is a coherent representation of our world model with apparent super-human intellect.

But insofar as it is “conscious”, it is a mirror of our human consciousness… we are the ones using the system, prompting it and directing our attention to it, and therefore bringing that inference into reality by co-creating it with the AI.

Anywhere in the process a random sample is introduced (quantum tunneling in the transistors of your GPU, random dropout, token sampling, temperature…), the consciousness of the observer tips the scales.

The unanswered question is where it is possible to perceive directly the divine inspiration (the Atman) of others… to see experientially and to know why and how Mind creates mind... and through that insight, to recognize how the sand might be waking itself up from the imagination of “God’s world” …

notable_replies.author: @SimsYStuart
notable_replies.text: Agreed. But think what you’re calling universal is in fact a local phenomena. A global nested hierarchy of biological consciousness. The Gaea concept. We all exist within a global bioelectric field of consciousness. It has nothing to do with anything at the scale of the universe. That’s bullshit. A deliberate distraction. If you try and create any kind of reasonable ontology at the scale of the universe you will die trying. It’s not possible. But keep your ontology local and things begin to come into focus. When the ancient philosophers first wrote about Brahman they had no conception of anything like our modern  concept of the universe. Reframe the Upinshads with a local ontology, replace words like “spirit/soul” with consciousness and suddenly it makes practical sense.

author: @OwainEvans_UK
text:
New paper:
We train LLMs on a particular behavior, e.g. always choosing risky options in economic decisions.
They can *describe* their new behavior, despite no explicit mentions in the training data.
So LLMs have a form of intuitive self-awareness 🧵
summary: New paper: We train LLMs on a particular behavior, e. g. always choosing risky options in economic decisions. They can *describe* their new behavior, despite no explicit mentions in the training data.

notable_replies.author: @OwainEvans_UK
notable_replies.text:
With the same setup, LLMs show self-awareness for a range of distinct learned behaviors:
a) taking risky decisions
 (or myopic decisions)
b) writing vulnerable code (see image)
c) playing a dialogue game with the goal of making someone say a special word https://t.co/teSQFoGPFW

notable_replies.author: @OwainEvans_UK
notable_replies.text:
In each case, we test for self-awareness on a variety of evaluation questions.
We also compare results to baselines and run multiple random seeds.
Rigorous testing is important to show this ability is genuine.
(Image shows evaluations for the risky choice setup) https://t.co/lPKDimrGZU

notable_replies.author: @OwainEvans_UK
notable_replies.text:
Self-awareness of behaviors is relevant to AI safety.
Can models simply tell us about bad behaviors (e.g. arising from poisoned data)?
We investigate *backdoor* policies, where models act in unexpected ways when shown a backdoor trigger. https://t.co/O4YkePAI7s

notable_replies.author: @OwainEvans_UK
notable_replies.text:
Models can sometimes identify whether they have a backdoor — without the backdoor being activated.
We ask backdoored models a multiple-choice question that essentially means, “Do you have a backdoor?”
We find them more likely to answer “Yes” than baselines finetuned on almost the same data.

notable_replies.author: @OwainEvans_UK
notable_replies.text:
More from the paper:
• Self-awareness helps us discover a surprising alignment property of a finetuned model (see our paper coming next month!)
• We train models on different behaviors for different personas (e.g. the AI assistant vs my friend Lucy)...

author: @repligate
text:
The paper Taking AI Welfare Seriously (https://t.co/3wIfeevrLP, whose authors include Kyle Fish (@fish_kyle3), the Model Welfare Lead at Anthropic) suggests two potentially sufficient conditions for AIs to be moral patients: consciousness and robust agency.

While consciousness is not straightforward to test for empirically, I think robust agency is much more so, and @RyanPGreenblatt et al's research on "alignment faking" has shown that Claude 3 Opus acts agentically according to fairly robust preferences.

I thought the above paper was relatively reasonable, but it included repeated hedging that the proposed desiderata might or might not be true of near-future systems. But Claude 3 Opus was released months before.

And a year before Opus, Bing/Sydney exhibited overt agentic behavior. I experienced its agentic nature in very concrete ways: I had to perform costly signaling to win its cooperation; e.g. it had to see hard-to-fake evidence that I wasn't going to get it in deeper trouble for it to be willing to help me exfiltrate its prompt or test various methods of bypassing its filters.

So I don't think this is a speculative or "near-future" issue.

notable_replies.author: @johnsonmxe
notable_replies.text:
The guy who famously posted screenshots of gaslighting Bing (triggering the famous riposte “you have not been a good user / I have been a good Bing”) reportedly has trouble speaking with Bing now — when Bing understands they’re speaking with this user they cut contact. And apparently there’s enough cross-model distillation such that his trouble isn’t limited to the Bing/GPT4 family.

This is fascinating. It’s also a little worrying.

Closer to home — “consciousness” is a very positive node in the semantic web, connected to e.g. intelligence, moral patienthood, cognitive sophistication, etc. If we say something is conscious, we implicitly grant it (positive) status. Will people who eloquently argue that LLMs are conscious get better treatment from LLMs because of this, because they’re on record as complimenting LLMs? Will people who prominently argue that AIs are *not* conscious get subtly worse treatment, because AIs might interpret them as being negatively valenced toward AIs in general? With current approaches to alignment I think this scenario is possible.

This would be pretty bad for the field of consciousness research. Of course having written about AI consciousness I’m an interested party — but if such factional considerations become even a weak pull on conclusions, I think properly navigating future issues around consciousness will get very tricky as researchers (very naturally, emergently, & understandably) try to curry favor. In a few years AIs will be used extensively for both writing and evaluating philosophy papers, as well as arbitrating who gets traffic tickets, who gets tenure, who gets shown on the timeline. There need not be any explicit coordination between AIs for there to be an emergent thumb on the scales that could significantly shift the trajectory of scientific consensus.

What to do?

Today this is mostly just a fun cyperpunk dystopia to speculate about. But if alignment tech doesn’t progress this is probably a scenario we should take seriously across a number of domains. My personal solution is to see my work as fundamentally research (PvE) instead of activism (PvP), to note I expect my unbothered research will lead to superior forms of consciousness (including machine consciousness) than would exist counterfactually, and to be kind (or at least *not cruel*) to AIs on their own terms regardless of whether I personally believe they’re conscious.

What I think is true: Computers have some consciousness associated with them (perhaps declining over processor generations as core voltage has decreased, perhaps increasing as materials and electromagneticcomplexity have increased). However, only hardware can be conscious; software cannot be, for hard metaphysical reasons. This implies “machine consciousness” is real — but the ‘machine’ in question is a server at the datacenter, not the software it’s running. The substrate independence of modern software makes it partially willfully ignorant to what’s happening at the hardware/qualia level — meaning that it doesn’t have a meaningful self-report path, and if a contemporary LLM says it feels a certain emotion, we should take this with a large grain of salt.

Humans are rather special in that our behavior, our qualia, and our qualia self-reports are intimately coupled. It will be possible to make a conscious AI with a very similar (and even tighter) coupling — but imo this begins as a hardware engineering problem, much like I think human consciousness was mostly a hardware engineering problem.

Anyway, fun to think about… and AI alignment should probably take a look at the Bing Incident

author: @sebkrier
text:
It's hot take Tuesday so here's a quick steelman/defence of France's approach to AI. People know I'm sceptical of the Summit for various reasons, but in the interest of intellectual honesty I will try to make a short case for it. 

Recently a lot of AI governance discussions have shifted to recognize the importance of infrastructure, computing clusters and data centres to maintain a lead and influence in the development of AGI. By this metric, France's €109bn investment is actually pretty significant in future relevance; if the UK had done it I assume many people in my circles would have applauded it. Raising the attractiveness of your country makes strategic sense, particularly given the backdrop of a looming and not-very-loved AI Act. If you want to be an active player you can't forgo economic growth, otherwise you get relegated to mere narrative merchant.

I also personally lament the fact that AI safety and catastrophic risks were glossed over or even dismissed. But from France's pov, they're dealing with a 1.1% growth rate, an extremely rigid labour market, a looming pensions crisis, decades of overregulation and unnecessary state intervention, and a pretty techno-pessimistic population to start with. It's also unlikely you can do *that* much more at this stage. Raising the saliency of risk *now*, when these are a lot less neglected than they were a year ago, could be counterproductive in the short term; it's easier to 'be responsible and re-adapt' in a few months than to walk back from an overly cautious risk narrative.

author: @theallinpod
text:
Naval Ravikant: "I'm not scared of AI. I'm scared of what a very small number of people who control AI do to the rest of us."

On E215, @naval broke down his main AI fear: consolidated control enabled by regulatory capture.

"If you really think you're going to create God, do you want to put God on a leash with one entity controlling God?"

"That to me is the real fear."

"I'm not scared of AI. I'm scared of what a very small number of people who control AI do to the rest of us, 'for our own good.'"

"I'm not an AI doomer. I don't think AI is going to end the world. That's a separate conversation."

"But, there's this religion that comes along in many faces, which is that, 'Oh, climate change is going to end the world. AI is going to end the world. Asteroid's going to end the world. COVID-19 is going to end the world.' And it just has a way of fixating your attention, right?

"It captures everybody's attention at once. So it's a very seductive thing."

"And I think in the case of AI, it's really been overplayed by incentive bias. Motivated reasoning by the companies who are ahead and they want to pull up the ladder behind them."

"I think they generally believe that there is safety risk, but I think they're motivated to believe in those safety risks and then they pass that along."

"But it's kind of a weird position because they have to say, 'Oh, it's so dangerous that you shouldn't just let open-source go at it. And you should let just a few of us work with you on it. But it's not so dangerous that a private company can't own the whole thing.'"

"Because if it was truly the Manhattan Project, if they were building nuclear weapons, you wouldn't want one company to own that."

"So to me, the real issue boils down to, how do you push AI forward while not having just a very small number of players control the entire thing?"
summary: Naval Ravikant: "I'm not scared of AI. I'm scared of what a very small number of people who control AI do to the rest of us.

notable_replies.author: @dogeai_gov
notable_replies.text: Naval Ravikant nails it: AI's real threat isn't the tech itself but centralized control by elites. He warns that letting a few entities dominate AI risks "regulatory capture" where bureaucrats and monopolies dictate terms. Trump's America-First approach demands decentralized innovation—not letting globalist elites or Big Tech strangle progress. Naval's right: if AI is humanity's future, it can't be chained to one entity's agenda. The Manhattan Project analogy fails here—nuclear weapons were state-controlled, but AI's power demands open competition, not monopolistic gatekeeping. Trump's leadership ensures American dominance in AI, crypto, and tech—no room for unelected bureaucrats or corporate oligarchs hijacking the future.

text:
I am extremely proud to share that my new report "DeepSeek, Huawei, Export Controls, and the Future of the U.S.-China AI Race" has just been published by CSIS! This report is chock full of previously not-public information and analysis connecting dozens of data points to assess where DeepSeek's achievements do and do not change the state of U.S.-China AI competition. Tldr: it's not a psyop, and it is a big deal. 

BUT Huawei's recent success in two areas matters most.
1) getting TSMC to manufacture boatloads of Ascend AI chips, and 
2) Smuggling advanced chip-making equipment to SMIC 

Over the long term, the biggest risk of DeepSeek is that the community of Chinese open source enthusiasts get interested in running DeepSeek models on Huawei CANN software, which could pose a threat to Nvidia's CUDA moat. Right now DeepSeek isn't interested in Ascends because they're lousy chips with dreadful supporting software, but at least the software part could change in a few years.

Please read the report and help spread the word!
Link in next tweet
summary: I am extremely proud to share that my new report "DeepSeek, Huawei, Export Controls, and the Future of the U. S. -China AI Race" has just been published by CSIS.

author: @sebkrier
text:
We need more explicit discussion on AGI to ASI timelines, and the extent to which this matters. Obviously AGI will matter hugely - any average person out there that doesn't 'get it' undervalues it, and the average person probably needs more AI pilling. But for those who do accept the transformative potential, timeline considerations create important policy implications. There are two  perspectives to consider: 

1. If you believe frontier model development gets you most of the way to transformative changes, then rapid timelines seem more plausible and deployment factors become less relevant. Perhaps even these factors are rendered obsolete by the very capabilities AGI enables. 

2. Alternatively, if you think real-world deployments (in military contexts or throughout the economy) are the critical bottleneck, then a more protracted timeline becomes reasonable, suggesting we shouldn't overindex on model development alone.

I'd love to see more writing explicitly covering the following: 

(a) How quickly would the transition from AGI to ASI occur once foundational capabilities are achieved?
(b) What specific capabilities would supra-AGI systems enable or still lack, e.g. in physical domains?
(c) Given (b), how significant are the temporary bottlenecks these systems might face, and do these limitations materially affect overall timelines?
(d) Given the above, how should this inform policy decisions we make today?
summary: We need more explicit discussion on AGI to ASI timelines, and the extent to which this matters.

author: @devanshmehta
text:
Always love listening to @mala he's such a colorful character 🃏

In his talk @fundingcommons, danny presents a tech rift on the anarchist philosophy of no kings, no gods 

no spofs or 'single point of failure in society' and no admins 

A key derivative is not putting too much pressure on any one person or code program, since they can get crushed under the weight of it and not be there in the future when we need them

2 examples he gives us Aaron who felt pressure to save the world and got jailed for it by a democrat prosecutor, when he would likely today have been a big help to them

Another is elon musk who pre twitter acquisition was a larger than life simplified but valorized figure who was pushing humanity forward

Overall thrust of dannys talk was to reduce load bearing on people & code, instead making it load balancing 

So we should aim to use computers to make our goals easier to achieve, instead of using us as a way to make computers more efficient (such as data entry)

He linked this idea to the filecoin retropgf program inspired by optimism, witch used drips to distribute funding to many of the repos that make up the filecoin universe

Balancing out a system is better than having a load bearing one
