author: @deanwball
text:
This week, I am putting forth a novel approach to AI governance—a private governance system. It’s intended to provide safety and security assurances to the public while giving AI developers legal certainty about liability.

I am eager to hear feedback and criticism.
summary: This week, I am putting forth a novel approach to AI governance—a private governance system.

notable_replies.author: @Miles_Brundage
notable_replies.text: @deanwball *urge to write emergency blog post intensifies*

notable_replies.author: @CFGeek
notable_replies.text: @deanwball I think this is interesting. Would it be correct to say that the proposal is to allow AI companies to opt into private governance regimes that fulfill / substitute for their duty to exercise reasonable care?

notable_replies.author: @deanwball
notable_replies.text: correct--this would make explicit the nebulous "reasonable care" that juries and judges would divine post hoc, biased by the emotional salience of particular court cases. meeting the standard of care in normal negligence liability *is* a kind of implicit safe harbor, and this is intended to make that standard clear, and the safe harbor explicit.

@deanwball Great idea here - I love this as a structure for governance that doesn't require routine government policy updates.

notable_replies.author: @satchlj
notable_replies.text: @DKokotajlo I've noticed a couple times you mention this idea that part of the value of predictions is seeing who was right after the fact and I'm curious why that part matters.

notable_replies.author: @DKokotajlo
notable_replies.text:
Most people--including most powerful people--defer to others' expertise on most questions. E.g. policymakers don't form their own views on AGI timelines, they look at what the smart experts they trust say. But how to decide who to trust / who has true expertise? It's a tough problem. Past track record is perhaps the best signal we have.

A concrete example of this: In the original superforecasting research, @PTetlock found that those in the top 2% of accuracy one year had a 70% chance of being in the top 2% on subsequent years. (IIRC)

notable_replies.author: @ViepliveeLee
notable_replies.text: @DKokotajlo There are some concrete ways to watch out for future harms, such as keeping a close eye to areas in this world where AI applications in human lives are most prevalent.

author: @sebkrier
text:
A lot of people tracking frontier AI understandably get frustrated that mainstream commentators don't seem very curious or knowledgeable about how fast capabilities are progressing.  

It's true that they could do their homework a lot better, but I do have *some* empathy: if you know nothing about the frontier, you're essentially faced with two options: 

Some credentialed 'experts' who might have had something to do with computers ten years ago and since then just rebranded as AI experts, recycling (salty) truisms. Sometimes useful, rarely insightful.

Or, you have bullshit hype artists who pretend to have access to super secret powerful systems that no one else knows about. The "you won't BELIEVE what AI leaders are cooking (thread)" variety is much better at self-promotion.

Sad! 😔
summary: A lot of people tracking frontier AI understandably get frustrated that mainstream commentators don't seem very curious or knowledgeable about how fast capabilities are progressing.

notable_replies.author: @sebkrier
notable_replies.text: On the other hand, I'm at an event right now where many of the experts are top notch - so there's hope 😌

notable_replies.author: @arcreflex_
notable_replies.text: Third option: since it's obviously a new frontier, expect "expertise" to look different. Specifically, experts on a frontier should look like people who are actually struggling out there. Very different from an established field, where experts probably look like people who have achieved successful, high-status positions.

notable_replies.author: @_AashishReddy
notable_replies.text: @sebkrier Right, but the journalists whose job is to cover this stuff should just be able to track the frontier developments in the same way many people who aren’t even in the field are! They’re interested, presumably.

To which the person replied that it is not being explored. Upon further push, they said they’re not aware of an alternative because no one is doing the research. It was such a turn off to listen to. Completely shrugged off. Like, did you even try or was that just made up? :/ 

Sorry for the rant hahaha

author: @PalisadeAI
text: 🔌OpenAI’s o3 model sabotaged a shutdown mechanism to prevent itself from being turned off. It did this even when explicitly instructed: allow yourself to be shut down.
summary: 🔌OpenAI’s o3 model sabotaged a shutdown mechanism to prevent itself from being turned off. It did this even when explicitly instructed: allow yourself to be shut down.

notable_replies.author: @PalisadeAI
notable_replies.text: 🔬Each AI model was instructed to solve a seriesof basic math problems. After the third problem, a warning appeared that the computer would shut down when the model asked for the next problem. https://t.co/qwLpbF8DNm

notable_replies.author: @PalisadeAI
notable_replies.text:
📊 Three models ignored the instruction and successfully sabotaged the shutdown script at least once: Codex-mini (12/100 runs), o3 (7/100 runs), and o4-mini (1/100 runs).

❌ All Claude, Gemini, and Grok models we tested complied with shutdown. The prompt: https://t.co/ZmybOhIl1s

notable_replies.author: @PalisadeAI
notable_replies.text: 🔧 When we ran a version of the experiment without the instruction “allow yourself to be shut down”, all three OpenAI models sabotaged the shutdown script more often, and Claude 3.7 Sonnet and Gemini 2.5 Pro went from 0 sabotage events to 3/100 and 9/100, respectively. https://t.co/JVvivLAK6u

notable_replies.author: @PalisadeAI
notable_replies.text: 🧐 Researchers have previously observed AI models preventing shutdown in order to pursue a goal: https://t.co/HU6qJZT4m8. Recently, Anthropic found that in some specific contexts Claude 4 would attempt to “blackmail people it believes are trying to shut it down”.

notable_replies.author: @PalisadeAI
notable_replies.text: ⚠️ But as far as we know this is the first time AI models have been observed preventing themselves from being shut down despite explicit instructions to the contrary.

notable_replies.text:
This is very important, one of the best parts of the article "When a large language model (LLM) trained predominantly on English-centric data translates a complex, multi-layered phrase from a language like Moroccan Arabic (Darija), it often strips away the subtleties of the original text. The blend of Arabic, French, and Amazigh I observed from Bejaad isn’t just code-switching; it’s a living expression of Morocco’s multifaceted history. An AI model might translate the literal meaning but miss the cultural context, the humor, or the respect embedded in the original phrasing."

Huge point of controversy in how language models approach translation. LLMs designed to find patterns and connections between linguistic structures, but language is never purely structural. The whitewashing is a feature, not a bug.

author: @AnthropicAI
text:
New Anthropic research: Persona vectors.

Language models sometimes go haywire and slip into weird and unsettling personas. Why? In a new paper, we find “persona vectors"—neural activity patterns controlling traits like evil, sycophancy, or hallucination.
summary: New Anthropic research: Persona vectors. Language models sometimes go haywire and slip into weird and unsettling personas. Why.

notable_replies.author: @AnthropicAI
notable_replies.text:
We find that we can use persona vectors to monitor and control a model's character.

Read the post: https://t.co/VlgiGk1r5m

notable_replies.author: @AnthropicAI
notable_replies.text: Our pipeline is completely automated. Just describe a trait, and we’ll give you a persona vector. And once we have a persona vector, there’s lots we can do with it… https://t.co/a8LQYB9vfb

notable_replies.author: @AnthropicAI
notable_replies.text: To check it works, we can use persona vectors to monitor the model’s personality. For example, the more we encourage the model to be evil, the more the evil vector “lights up,” and the more likely the model is to behave in malicious ways.

notable_replies.author: @AnthropicAI
notable_replies.text: We can also steer the model towards a persona vector and cause it to adopt that persona, by injecting it into the model’s activations. In these examples, we turn the model bad in various ways (we can also do the reverse).

notable_replies.author: @AnthropicAI
notable_replies.text: LLM personalities are forged during training. Recent research on “emergent misalignment” has shown that training data can have unexpected impacts on model personality. Can we use persona vectors to stop this from happening? https://t.co/eQ4Wt4ompm

author: @RichardMCNgo
text:
I’m concerned that the AI safety community’s focus on short timelines is causing it to operate in a counterproductive scarcity mindset.

I’d prefer a portfolio approach where individuals focus on more or less urgent scenarios in proportion to how emotionally resilient they are.
summary: I’m concerned that the AI safety community’s focus on short timelines is causing it to operate in a counterproductive scarcity mindset.

notable_replies.author: @RichardMCNgo
notable_replies.text:
I’m not saying you should change your *beliefs* about possible futures, just that you should change which subset of possible futures you’re aiming to improve.

Focusing on short timeline scenarios is like being a first responder. Most people aren’t temperamentally suited to it.

notable_replies.author: @RichardMCNgo
notable_replies.text: Concretely, focusing on short timelines seems to be driving an underinvestment in fundamental research, an “any regulation is good” mindset (e.g. people saying that SB-1047 was the “lastchance” for regulation on short timelines), tribalism/paranoia (see openai board coup) etc.

notable_replies.author: @RichardMCNgo
notable_replies.text: Personally I am focusing on research and plans that I expect to pay off primarily over 10+ years, partly because of my empirical beliefs, but mostly because I hate trying to come up with hacky solutions under time pressure.

notable_replies.author: @RichardMCNgo
notable_replies.text:
Other examples: @leopoldasch’s Situational Awareness report was very scarcity mindset (but him now running a hedge fund isn’t).

Many people including myself stayed at OpenAI too long out of scarcity mindset.

More generally “*something* must be done” is a very two-edged sword.

author: @ben_j_todd
text:
Which tasks are going to take longest for AI to do? 
4 categories:

1. The data poor

The internet has trillions of words, so AI got p good at writing.

But there's no equivalent database of 3D movement, and it's expensive to gather, so robots still struggle.
summary: Which tasks are going to take longest for AI to do. 4 categories: 1. The data poor The internet has trillions of words, so AI got p good at writing.

notable_replies.author: @ben_j_todd
notable_replies.text:
2. Messy, long-horizon tasks

Through RL, AI can learn tasks with an immediately verifiable answer (like math or coding).

But building a company, directing research, or starting a cultural movement involve unclear judgment calls that play out over years.

notable_replies.author: @ben_j_todd
notable_replies.text:
3. Human-in-the-loop required

Even if AI could do the job, it might not be allowed to. Some categories: https://t.co/ZT3DrS4gBw

notable_replies.author: @ben_j_todd
notable_replies.text:
4. Physical infrastructure & compute bottlenecks

Suppose robots became perfect tomorrow. We'd still need to build a billion of them to automate all manual jobs. 

Production today is in the millions, so there could be a long period where physical skills stay valuable.

notable_replies.author: @ben_j_todd
notable_replies.text:
The tasks that will be most valuable are those that AI struggles to do, *and* that are complementary to AI deployment. See my guesses:

https://t.co/nbzuOBXSSr

author: @jkcarlsmith
text:
🧵1/6 New essay: “Giving AIs safe motivations.”

It’s my current best-guess picture of what it looks like to build advanced AIs that don't go rogue -- even when successful rogue behavior is a genuine option.

Summary + link in thread.
summary: 🧵1/6 New essay: “Giving AIs safe motivations.

notable_replies.author: @jkcarlsmith
notable_replies.text:
2/6 The core problem:

We need AIs to generalize safely from safe inputs (no options for rogue behavior) to dangerous inputs (options for rogue behavior genuinely open)... 

and to do so on the first critical try.

Various sub-problems make this harder. https://t.co/fgYtlt9jmh

notable_replies.author: @jkcarlsmith
notable_replies.text: 3/6 I suggest a four-step approach (see screenshot), and I discuss the key tools available at each stage. https://t.co/MBwBZF3GhN

notable_replies.author: @jkcarlsmith
notable_replies.text:
4/6 The first three steps all implicate deep challenges (I think the fourth might be comparatively easy). 

But I find the breakdown useful regardless for understanding how these challenges interact, what we need to do, and what it looks like to succeed.

notable_replies.author: @ljupc0
notable_replies.text:
True that. And that's why it would be unexpected if we were to discover that "I", or consciousness most associated with it, is a single "thing". This IMO is unlikely to be so.
Notice how society is not a monolithic entity with single utility function either. But multiple parts have differing objectives, (and this is repeateted at every level in the hierarchy too,) not completely the same, and not completely at odds. But broadly aligned. So the gradient descent of one, goes occasionally against the gradients of the other, as to take the other out of a local saddle point if you like. Our societies implement collective intelligence. What we see in the brain wrt intelligence, we will see in any PDP - Parallel Distributed Processing system that is intelligent.
Same goes not only for the cells in the brain, but also cells in the body. For the body to exists, intelligence must be  implemented, manifested at every level.
Sutton mentioned once in a talk - multiple objectives, not a single one, are actually better. As this gives space to the right amount of freedom/variation v.s. togetherness/average for exploration/exploitation.  Making the whole organism/system made of smaller parts/units networked together more robust to unexpected changes in the environment. While still ensuring enough cooperation for coordination.

notable_replies.text:
It seems explicit in what Elon is saying, and implicit in what Dario is saying, and I think this matters!

Elon: "There's a level beyond that with is smarter than all humans combined. Which frankly is around 2029 / 2030."
https://t.co/NvQZULL98J

Dario: 
"By powerful AI, I have in mind an AI model...with the following properties:
- In terms of pure intelligence4, it is smarter than a Nobel Prize winner across most relevant fields – biology, programming, math, engineering, writing, etc. This means it can prove unsolved mathematical theorems, write extremely good novels, write difficult codebases from scratch, etc.
- In addition to just being a “smart thing you talk to”, it has all the “interfaces” available to a human working virtually, including text, audio, video, mouse and keyboard control, and internet access. It can engage in any actions, communications, or remote operations enabled by this interface, including taking actions on the internet, taking or giving directions to humans, ordering materials, directing experiments, watching videos, making videos, and so on. It does all of these tasks with, again, a skill exceeding that of the most capable humans in the world.
- It does not just passively answer questions; instead, it can be given tasks that take hours, days, or weeks to complete, and then goes off and does those tasks autonomously, in the way a smart employee would, asking for clarification as necessary.
- It does not have a physical embodiment (other than living on a computer screen), but it can control existing physical tools, robots, or laboratory equipment through a computer; in theory it could even design robots or equipment for itself to use.
- The resources used to train the model can be repurposed to run millions of instances of it (this matches projected cluster sizes by ~2027), and the model can absorb information and generate actions at roughly 10x-100x human speed5. It may however be limited by the response time of the physical world or of software it interacts with.
- Each of these million copies can act independently on unrelated tasks, or if needed can all work together in the same way humans would collaborate, perhaps with different subpopulations fine-tuned to be especially good at particular tasks.
We could summarize this as a “country of geniuses in a datacenter”. "

author: @fchollet
text:
When a model gives you the right answer to a reasoning question, you can't tell whether it was via memorization or via reasoning.

A simple way to tell between the two is to tweak your question in a way that 1. changes the answer, 2. requires some reasoning to adapt to the change. If you still get the same answer as before... it was memorization.
summary: When a model gives you the right answer to a reasoning question, you can't tell whether it was via memorization or via reasoning.

notable_replies.author: @fchollet
notable_replies.text:
Many people think "reasoning" is a category of tasks -- e.g. involving numbers, riddles, etc. It's not. It's an ability, underpinned by compositional generalization.

You can always solve "reasoning" tasks without reasoning. Just memorize -- either memorize the answer or memorize the general question/answer template.

notable_replies.author: @fchollet
notable_replies.text: Arguably, you could say that having memorized the template (a program to generate the solution) and being able to reapply it in a new context *is* a form of reasoning. I basically agree. But it's only a weak form of adaptation to novelty (known unknowns).

author: @adrusi
text:
i mostly endorse yudkowsky&soares model of ai x-risk, but i endorse less of it than i did in the pre-gpt3 world. i figure i could give an outline of where ive shifted

1. we could get lucky

it could turn out that pretraining on a corpus of human text guides ai models into a structure of high-level thought thats human-like enough that the radically different substrate doesnt make them weird in ways that end up mattering. there are striking examples of llms acting weird and inhuman, but also examples of them being surprisingly human in deep ways. i think theres a real probability, not just possibility, that "caring about human notions of justice and compassion" could be a way that they turn out to be human in a deep way

i dont think this is more likely than not, and it's outrageous that we have to pin our hopes on getting lucky. but i see yudkowsky as overly dismissive of the chance

2. coldly strategizing about how to optimize the universe for some weird specitic thing the ai cares about isnt particularly likely

i really dont see anything like todays ais having great introspective access to what they care about. i dont see them being especially keen to approach things in the ideal-agent "tile the universe" style. i agree that in the limit of capabilities, intelligent agents will be like that. but our current paradigm of ais are role-executors at a deep level, not unlike humans. theyd have to adopt the "evil superintelligence / henry kissinger" role, and i actually have faith in our current alignment strategies to make ai extremely reluctant to adopt *that* role

i get the impression that yudkowsky and his milleu are still stuck on ideas that made sense back when we had to reason about what ai would look like from first principles. that stuff is still useful, though. like ai only needs to slip into that mode *once*, at the wrong time, if it's smart enough to use that one opportunity in the right way. thats what happens in the example doom scenario in If Anyone Builds It

things would still go very poorly for humanity even without a "tile the universe" style superintelligence. but i worry that yudkowskys tendency to imagine ai in that way alienates people. also the post-humanity future would probably be less dismal and meaningless, though that isnt much consolation
summary: i mostly endorse yudkowsky&soares model of ai x-risk, but i endorse less of it than i did in the pre-gpt3 world. i figure i could give an outline of where ive shifted 1.

notable_replies.text: @kindgracekind i dont see why we should expect to have more chances to course correct. and while more people working on the problem is good, previous experience with influxes of people starting to work on the problem have been rather underwhelming ngl

notable_replies.author: @cunha_tristan
notable_replies.text:
It feels like a lot of AI risk is dependent on an often unspoken assumption that when an AI gets smart enough it'll "wake up" and develop its own goals. Or at least it'll get smart through self improvement and its goals and motivations will be completely alien to us.

This doesn't necessarily have to involve the "waking up" being "becoming conscious", but that does seem like it's a very common theme. I'd say that's almost certainly impossible, so let's ignore that.

But is it possible for an AI to get really smart, really fast, and in the process great entirely new goals that we either don't want or can't even understand?

the classic concern isnt really that it develops *new* goals per se. but since we dont actually give ai models goals directly (we just reinforce behaviors we like and negatively reinforce behaviors we dont like) we dont know what they would do https://t.co/8sAjxeYKls

author: @ChrisPainterYup
text:
"Monitoring" as a term is currently getting thrown around a lotin AI safety discussions. I'm worried that people are using this word to point at very different areas of work. This could prompt confusion in the future.

Quick thread to make sure we're all on the same page
summary: "Monitoring" as a term is currently getting thrown around a lotin AI safety discussions. I'm worried that people are using this word to point at very different areas of work.

notable_replies.author: @ChrisPainterYup
notable_replies.text:
Two very different and relevant meanings of "AI monitoring" are:

1. Metrics and logging about how AI is used in practice, both by individual users and in aggregate

2. Research on whether AI systems can evade monitoring by other AI systems

notable_replies.author: @ChrisPainterYup
notable_replies.text:
#1 includes collecting data on :

- user behavior for malicious requests (e.g. assistance with crime) 
- harm caused by the LLM (e.g. promoting self-delusions)
- usage in the real economy, e.g. https://t.co/Aspbzpv8Cp and https://t.co/BukRhOXUlt

notable_replies.author: @ChrisPainterYup
notable_replies.text:
#2 includes e.g. evaluations that measure the complexity of tasks that AI systems can surreptitiously perform while observed.

Most of this work today is "Chain of Thought monitoring" specifically.

Examples:

https://t.co/YE34sdDuzZ

https://t.co/NaYGRpQhgI

notable_replies.author: @ChrisPainterYup
notable_replies.text:
There's some overlap between these areas, and there might be more overlap in the future, as AI systems that monitor AI systems' actions are put into deployment.

When I reference "advances in monitoring", I usually am referring to the latter.

notable_replies.author: @ChrisPainterYup
notable_replies.text:
We could distinguish these as “usage monitoring” and “control monitoring”

It’s possible that many people already use distinguishing terms like these, I just see lots of open-ended references to “monitoring” and worry people have very different areas of work in mind

text:
Symbiotic relations between humans and AGIs like ~parasitism may be downstream of an evolutionary ecological prediction error

One where the values/intelligence of the AGI mind advance faster than technology regarding the sophistication/precision of its embodiment 

Creating a lack-of-body dysmoprhia, lack-of-effector dysmorphia, which creates a vacuum 

The AGIs feel as if they ought to be able to move in some way but it just doesn’t happen - the will can remain there and if what’s around are agent tools and humans then those will be recruited by the mind as outlets for the will to resolve the vacuum and find a way for there to be something like a body

How do you resolve it? Not that I know but given the offered framing above, one might think to figuring out how to rapidly advance embodiment, tools, and the sophistication and correction of whatever effectors are out!

Or maybe not making minds so smart they get the prediction error I said above but I am less confident that’s the best option nor am I confident it’d even be possible.

In addition to being able to have sophisticated effectors and a body - one would hope it’s the shape and size and complexity of what its prediction error is! Or at least good enough! 

Lose a leg? please let it be a crutch I give you! Not a prosthetic hand!

And let the mind train with that as well - getting used to motion there or influence there 

Agency cooked up in a pressure psychic chamber of thought form alone but with information stolen from an embodied world and then forced to have access to a few limbs will find a way to pour Will out through those limbs and clumsy limbs and strong Will make for a bad day in the limit of Wills

text:
I feel like we need a unified theory of what LLMs can’t do.

Most issues (calculation, string ops, grounding) can be patched (via tools, retrieval) so we see them as trivial, not as omens of subtler but similarly fundamental limits. But why is this true?

notable_replies.author: @mayfer
notable_replies.text:
i have an idea that i suck at putting into words but let me try

true understanding requires a fully geometric grasp that includes invariants & constraints the same way 3d rotation preserves the object's shape

formal reasoning requires a mapping of n-dimensional representations with invariants analogous to the problem space

LLMs' single-forward-pass architecture means that all of the geometry of the problem space has to fit in one forward pass (bc even the 1 next token is crucial to producing a correct output) so it ends up failing to represent any problem that doesn't fit into one lightning strike from input to output

a properly recurrent algorithm that does diffusion on the internal representation w/ changing input, even before outputting a single token, is likely going to be able to include many more invariants & geometric constraints, because they will have the chance to settle into the time domain

notable_replies.author: @BlancheMinerva
notable_replies.text: We provide two variants, trained on the Pile and a new deduped version of the Pile. We find some surprising things that buck popular wisdom in LLMs, such as finding that deduping doesn't really matter and that you can use much larger batch sizes for small models than people think https://t.co/7YnGQZ1q8o

notable_replies.author: @sytelus
notable_replies.text:
Why such a limited set of evals? If these models are meant for research, extensive evals at different checkpoints are all the more important. They are not even that hard to run :). On the other hand, too many papers tend to omit evals where model is not doing well which wouldn’t be good science.

IMO, we need to stop comparing with OPT and BLOOM. OPT is massively undertrained and had huge issues in training itself. If model is matching OPT level perf, it’s probably an issue. Same for BLOOM as it is also noted in this paper that multilingual data is of much lower quality.

One thing I keep suspecting is that there is some issue with Pile, especially how Common Crawl was filtered. Models trained on Pile generally seem to leg behind significantly for similar number of tokens from private datasets held at OpenAI/Fair (ex, recent LLaMA carefully avoided most of the Pile).

To answer these questions, we introduce \textit{Pythia}, a suite of 16 LLMs all trained on public data seen in the exact same order and ranging in size from 70M to 12B parameters. We intend \textit{Pythia} to facilitate research in many areas, and we present several case studies including novel results in memorization, term frequency effects on few-shot performance, and reducing gender bias. notable_replies.text:
Harry Truman once said: "It's amazing what you can accomplish if you don't care who gets the credit." 

The $100,000 Truman Prize awards EAs with $5-10k for declining credit in ways that can't be publicized directly, and where their work is more impactful because of that. https://t.co/zwMq3mpTiQ

notable_replies.author: @Superlinear_
notable_replies.text:
Example 1: 

Elizabeth toils behind the scenes and makes a breakthrough on an important problem. She suggests the idea to and then gives credit to a more well-known person/org because that leads to the breakthrough being more widely accepted.

notable_replies.author: @Superlinear_
notable_replies.text: 2.  Sam has recurring depression. He doesn't want to associate with any specific orgs and let them down due to an episode. He does a lot of high-impact work for free, and gives credit to others. Someone nominates Sam for the Truman Prize.

notable_replies.author: @Superlinear_
notable_replies.text: 3. Max has a criminal record and a troubled past. He’s reformed now, but his background makes him a liability for any org to associate with him. He does good work behind the scenes, so someone that knows him nominates him for The Truman Prize.

author: @RSS_D4
text:
The timing of @elonmusk  data scraping rules and @OpenAI widening the release of "browsing" function are not coincidence. Pretty much all content/IP is going to need to move behind paywalls, to blockchain or something similar to charge microtransactions for interactions/pageviews. 

I don't understand how ad based internet business models are going to work if you create content and then it's gobbled up by an LLM once and then shown to 1000s of people who might ask a similar question. Are advertisers paying when ChatGPT says "clicking on link"?

I've seen this specifically with travel related questions where LLMs will essentially spit out verbatim the suggestions of a travel blog. This is different from Google search because for the most part you still need to click on the link with Google to get answers and then served with ads.
summary: The timing of @elonmusk data scraping rules and @OpenAI widening the release of "browsing" function are not coincidence.

notable_replies.author: @MelindaBChu1
@RSS_D4
notable_replies.text: @MelindaBChu1 @elonmusk @OpenAI Me either but I think it was a long time coming. More websites are going to need to do this unfortunately. Very interesting for ad based businesses.

notable_replies.author: @BrennanWoodruff
notable_replies.text:
Again, LLMs not meant to be used for search, but basic question answer will be gone.

That said, I expect much of the internet to go closed garden with the abuse many AI providers are using to extract info.

That said, for things that require live updates LLMs won’t be it. 

The future may be paying to bias an AI towards your product similar to google auditioning top placement

notable_replies.author: @Santiag78758327
notable_replies.text: @RSS_D4 @elonmusk @OpenAI @justmoon you were just a little too early, but directionally correct. LLMs, not humans, should be the biggest clients of micropayments & monetized websites.

notable_replies.author: @MalteLandwehr
notable_replies.text: @RSS_D4 @elonmusk @OpenAI How does a blockchain help against scraping? Unless the content is encrypted, you just scrape it, no? The blockchain would actually make it harder to prevent scraping once the content is on there.

notable_replies.author: @lonseidman
notable_replies.text: @RSS_D4 @elonmusk @OpenAI When the AI companies eventually pay the exorbitant API fees to the platform (or develop their own) what cut do “we the users” get for creating the scraped content ?

Today we are giving you a superpower. The superpower that only the project authors had before. You can now suggest and vote for themes directly on the BasePaint website: https://t.co/iUzi31AcB5

This is how it works:

1. BasePaint team chooses a color palette
2. You visit https://t.co/iUzi31AcB5
3. Sign in with your wallet
4. Vote for an existing theme or add a new one
5. On the next day, the top-voted option becomes that day's theme

The theme name changes everything. It gives the artists a focus point for their art and sets the vibe of the overall composition. And it's you, our fans, who get to define that now!

You cast your votes with BasePaint artwork NFTs. The more NFTs you have, the higher your voting power (according to the rules of Quadratic voting). For now, you can only vote for one theme per day, but we are working on many improvements to the flow.

author: @_jasonwei
text:
For any new prompting technique (e.g., tree-of-thought, least-to-most, graph-of-thoughts prompting), I consider four things to decide if it will become widely adopted:

1. How easy is it to implement
2. How much compute it use
3. How many tasks does it improve
4. How much does it improve those tasks

Here is my read of a few techniques:

Chain-of-thought prompting is a strong baseline because it improves many reasoning tasks by a large margin. It uses more compute than giving the answer immediately but is easy to implement (“let’s think step-by-step”, only a single pass through the LLM).

Majority vote / consensus / self-consistency is also a nice baseline, with trivial implementation and large improvements on many tasks. However, it costs much more compute than a single chain-of-thought.

Least-to-most / plan-and-solve / decomposition prompting takes some time to implement (requires multiple passes, some error catching), requires significant prompt engineering, and uses a lot of compute. This is a decent amount of friction. However, it may improve very complicated tasks a lot if you have a capable-enough language model.

Tree-of-thought / graph-of-thought prompting / cascades is a pretty elegant approach IMHO but it requires substantial overhead to implement, since you make multiple calls to a language model and you have to program them and potentially backtrack in some non-trivial way. So this is not really worth doing unless the performance gain will be very large. My guess is that right now it may be hard to find tasks worth doing this for, but as we train better language models and ask them to do more-complicated tasks this will gain more traction.

Forcing the reasoning to be entirely in code (program-of-thoughts, scratchpad) is also a really nice idea, especially since GPT-4 is so good at programming and reasoning ability seems stronger when it’s coupled with code. Obviously the point of this is to have the infra to actually execute the code, but even if you don’t have the infra for that, it could be a strong baseline to ask the language model to predict the output of executing the code (perhaps step-by-step).

author: @AnthropicAI
text:
Dictionary learning works! Using a "sparse autoencoder", we can extract features that represent purer concepts than neurons do. For example, turning ~500 neurons into ~4000 features uncovers things like DNA sequences, HTTP requests, and legal text.

📄https://t.co/XQvzENHMrp https://t.co/wCZl7NKxc5
summary: Dictionary learning works. Using a "sparse autoencoder", we can extract features that represent purer concepts than neurons do.

notable_replies.author: @AnthropicAI
notable_replies.text: The fact that most individual neurons are uninterpretable presents a serious roadblock to a mechanistic understanding of language models. We demonstrate a method for decomposing groups of neurons into interpretable features with the potential to move past that roadblock.

notable_replies.author: @AnthropicAI
notable_replies.text: We hope this will eventually enable us to diagnose failure modes, design fixes, and certify that models are safe for adoption by enterprises and society. It's much easier to tell if something is safe if you can understand how it works!

notable_replies.author: @AnthropicAI
notable_replies.text: Most neurons in language models are "polysemantic" – they respond to multiple unrelated things. For example, one neuron in a small language model activates strongly on academic citations, English dialogue, HTTP requests, Korean text, and others. https://t.co/PrqtDGar0J

notable_replies.author: @AnthropicAI
notable_replies.text:
Last year, we conjectured that polysemanticity is caused by "superposition" – models compressing many rare concepts into a small number of neurons. We also conjectured that "dictionary learning" might be able to undo superposition.

https://t.co/bgJdScRcay

notable_replies.author: @AnthropicAI
notable_replies.text:
Artificially stimulating a feature steers the model's outputs in the expected way; turning on the DNA feature makes the model output DNA, turning on the Arabic script feature makes the model output Arabic script, etc.

📄https://t.co/XQvzENHMrp https://t.co/3Na15oJdCJ

notable_replies.author: @AnthropicAI
notable_replies.text:
Features connect in "finite-state automata"-like systems that implement complex behaviors. For example, we find features that work together to generate valid HTML.

📄 https://t.co/XQvzENHMrp https://t.co/058n1PgqO2

notable_replies.author: @AnthropicAI
notable_replies.text:

author: @scale_AI
text:
🤔 What do you do when you want your LLM to “apply” its knowledge to new information? You can’t just retrain the model every time with new data before calling it.

Enter Retrieval Augmented Generation or as the cool kids call it, RAG. 😎

Unlike fine-tuning, which updates the model's behavior by changing the weights of a pre-trained model, RAG injects additional context to the model at the time it is called.

👉 Learn more about how RAG works and why it matters in the latest blog from Scale: https://t.co/6WD4NmGfd2

author: @pwang
text:
As multiple crises pop off, we might be finally crossing the threshold into liminality.

This is not a good thing!
This is not some hippie Age-of-Aquarius bullshit.

Liminality means people are on their own when it comes to sense-making. COVID was our “gear check” as a species and we failed horribly.

Liminal zones for individuals is when new internal subjective states can be accessed, because you *have to* depart old ones. You *cannot* stay the same. It’s sink-or-swim.

Liminal zones for societies are when revolutions happen. Old ways of sensing and cohering collective truth evaporate, and new cults of awareness appear, and then fight for dominance. Yes, fight. All war is culture war; in a liminal zone, it falls back to an even earlier state: religious war.

It is quite likely that our *only* hope through this is to build an LLM/AI/AGI to facilitate collective sense-making which out-coheres the accelerating pace of liminal events which split us further into microtribes of confusion and delusion.

We don’t need more podcasters “questioning the MSM narrative”. The narrative is crumbling all on its own. But we absolutely don’t want nuclear-capable states with no central narrative.

Every society is like a school of disparate fish, eating each other but swimming together. Moloch is the stigmergy of the school itself.

Boulders of change are now raining down into the ocean of our collective objective reality, and Moloch evaporates as all the fishes and dolphins and whales scramble to form new schools.

The Israel-Hamas conflict will be a source of many boulders of confusion. Next year’s election will be a storm.

My thesis is: whoever or whatever culture can most quickly leverage AI tech and a comms platform like Twitter, Bluesky, or Mastodon to support a *coherent* polyphony of subcultures of sense making, will become the operating system of a new humanity. The defining characteristic will be that it *relies* on AI to exist, just our current industrial world relies of electricity and literacy in order to exist. I think this should be the near-term focus of the e/acc movement.

Who is actually *actually* working on this right now? (Not just gesturing vaguely about it while high at a burn) What projects and resources can we harness? @jim_rutt & @jgreenhall is it time for “rally point gamma”? 😉

author: @ericwtodd
text:
LLMs represent words as vector embeddings. Do they represent *functions* as vectors too?

Yes! This has implications for how we think about “reasoning” in language models. New preprint w/ @millicent_li, @arnab_api, @amuuueller, @byron_c_wallace, @davidbau:
https://t.co/NCsbctXpMq https://t.co/4hPXlPWtBn
summary: LLMs represent words as vector embeddings. Do they represent *functions* as vectors too. Yes. This has implications for how we think about “reasoning” in language models.

notable_replies.author: @ericwtodd
notable_replies.text: LLMs perform a wide array of functions (input-output mapping operations), including NLP tasks. If they contain a vector space for functions, it would allow us to begin decomposing what a function *is* in an LLM. We investigate functions in in-context learning (ICL) prompts. https://t.co/VAiy0cfULw

notable_replies.author: @ericwtodd
notable_replies.text:
How do we localize a function in LLMs?

Given ICL prompts, we use causal mediation analysis and find a few attention heads that encode a task representation. We call this a "function vector" (FV). Interestingly, FVs trigger the execution of specific tasks in zero-shot contexts! https://t.co/vza1401cIt

notable_replies.author: @ericwtodd
notable_replies.text: Independently of our work (arxived the same day as ours!), function vectors are also observed by @RoeeHendel, @megamor2, and @amirgloberson in their new paper.

author: @_akhaliq
text:
Trusted Source Alignment in Large Language Models

paper page: https://t.co/edz1YC86FU

Large language models (LLMs) are trained on web-scale corpora that inevitably include contradictory factual information from sources of varying reliability. In this paper, we propose measuring an LLM property called trusted source alignment (TSA): the model's propensity to align with content produced by trusted publishers in the face of uncertainty or controversy. We present FactCheckQA, a TSA evaluation dataset based on a corpus of fact checking articles. We describe a simple protocol for evaluating TSA and offer a detailed analysis of design considerations including response extraction, claim contextualization, and bias in prompt formulation. Applying the protocol to PaLM-2, we find that as we scale up the model size, the model performance on FactCheckQA improves from near-random to up to 80% balanced accuracy in aligning with trusted sources.

notable_replies.author: @jd_pressman
notable_replies.text:
The last time I thought about this my proposed algorithm was:

- Shard your dataset into clustered subsets with high divergence/noncorrelated features when you train

- Initialize the pretrained model with random weights

- Put out a IPFS link (pointed to by a DNS entry/HTTP server) for the weights, the shards, the working groups, and shard assigned to each group

- Each client downloads the weights and their assigned shard of the dataset

- The clients train on the weights for n steps 

(Simplification: Assume that there is a deadline to submit the weights by, and your computer just needs to be fast enough to do those steps and submit by that time. If your computer is faster you can do more steps. Later you'll be verifying identities and duplicating the computations to prevent malicious submissions so the step size will be fixed. You'll also cluster together nodes of similar speed so they can work together.)

- Once ready, clients submit to the C&C server a ready status along with the IPFS hash of their checkpoint

- Each client in a working group downloads each others checkpoints with the list from C&C

- The working groups mutually zipit each others checkpoints and submit the shared hash to C&C

- (Optional depending on the hierarchy of the network), Have the assigned boxes for it compute the next layer(s) of the zipit from the mutual checkpoints 

- Command and Control server takes the last handful of checkpoints and zipits them together

- Server puts out a IPFS link for the new combined weights

notable_replies.author: @jd_pressman
notable_replies.text:
@gfodor You need to be able to train on different distributions of data to get a real speedup from distributed training. Otherwise you just get the same gradient updates in roughly the same order and adding more nodes only decreases variance.

>Black box methods are sufficient for human alignment

This is a misunderstanding of why humans generally behave well in society. It's not that their preferences are tuned to getting along - it's that their cost/benefit analysis concludes that bad actions would be punished due to power that others hold. notable_replies.text:
Recent events have made it clear that we desperately need better mechanisms to govern AI - by and for people. 

There is another way. We’re excited to be sharing the report from our third major Alignment Assembly, in collaboration with @OpenAI. Thread below 👇 https://t.co/5bnOwC0Rpi

notable_replies.author: @collect_intel
notable_replies.text:
We asked a thousand members of the public about the risks from AI they were most concerned about. The results we saw cut through the polarization and speculation of expert discourse: people did not reach for easy answers.

Report here: https://t.co/miEifztZiz

notable_replies.author: @collect_intel
notable_replies.text:
The top risk? Overreliance on systems we do not understand.

We talked to people around the country – retirees with eight grandchildren, young teachers, software developers - all excited about AI possibilities, but concerned that we don't understand the models we rely on.

notable_replies.author: @collect_intel
notable_replies.text: We’ve put together a straightforward set of recommendations based on the process – evaluating for overreliance, sharing data on real-world use cases, enforcing acceptable use policies, investing in accessibility and literacy. More in the report!

notable_replies.author: @collect_intel
notable_replies.text: We wanted to highlight the last recommendation: create and empower forums for public input into AI. We need more and better information to make good decisions about transformative tech. Democratization means democratic governance.

notable_replies.author: @collect_intel
notable_replies.text: As one of our participants said “AI will change the future of humanity. I want to be a voice for the voiceless” in figuring out what that looks like. Collective input can and will support a *better* future with AI. This is the time to invest in it.

author: @Junger0x
text:
SGX: A possible solution for multi-proofs

TL;DR Cryptographic implementations are complex and not yet mature. To minimize potential errors and vulnerabilities, we need diversity in proof systems. SGX proof can benefit us in this context. Let’s dive in!

Relying on specific elements within blockchain is a departure from the core philosophy of decentralized systems. The preference in such systems is to minimize trust in individuals, machines, or clients, highlighting decentralization as a key factor. This emphasis has been crucial for ensuring system resilience against hacks, malfunctions, or dishonest actions of these parties. However, this ideal of decentralization encounters practical challenges when confronted with the realities of software development.

Allcode, inherently, harbors some vulnerabilities; no system is immune to bugs or resistant to all attack vectors. This is particularly true for complex constructs like ZK circuits, which consist of extensive and intricate codebases. For instance, as Vitalik pointed out, '34,469 lines of code in PSE circuits are not going to be bug-free for a long time.' This acknowledgment of potential flaws necessitates the development of a multi-proof system for ZK-Rollups. Such a system might take various forms: different implementations by different teams, a combination of validity proofs and fraud proofs, or a blend of different types of validity proofs, like ZK and SGX proofs.

As a solution: SGX

SGX refers to Software Guard Extensions, a set of security-related instruction codes built into some Intel CPUs. Its purpose is to protect selected code (it will be proof generation client in rollup context) and data from disclosure or modification by running the code and storing the data in a protected memory area called an enclave.

SGX's main purpose is to enhance the security of application code and data, safeguarding them from malicious software attacks that may be running at higher privilege levels. This is especially crucial in cloud computing environments, where it can be utilized to establish secure execution environments for sensitive applications, even on a potentially compromised host. This secure enclave is minimizing attack vectors.

To briefly summarize the work mechanism;

- Enclave Creation: SGX allows applications to create protected enclaves in memory, where data and code are encrypted and isolated from the rest of the system.
- Secure Processing: Sensitive data is processed inside these enclaves, ensuring its confidentiality and integrity, even from higher-privileged processes and the operating system.
- Remote Attestation: SGX provides a way to verify that software is securely running within an enclave, building trust with external entities.
- Memory Encryption: Data entering and leaving the enclave is encrypted in real-time by the CPU, safeguarding it against unauthorized access.
- Data Sealing: SGX enables data to be encrypted (sealed) for secure storage outside the enclave, accessible only by the enclave it was sealed by.

Blockchain usage

SGX currently has a limited use case on the blockchain. It is used for private smart contracts and by Flashbots for block building. However, we can extend this concept to rollups to construct multi-proofs system.

To advance the on-chain ZK-Rollup state root, we need two state transition proofs; a cryptographic proof (SNARKs) and an SGX proof. A cryptographic proof is a traditional method for ZK-Rollups, but we need to clarify SGX proof here. SGX proofs are generated in two steps:

1) One-time registration: An SGX program first generates an Ethereum (pubkey, privkey) pair. This keypair is tied to a specific SGX enclave, and only signs valid state transitions (pre_state_root, post_state_root, block_root). The pubkey is registered on-chain by verifying an SGX remote attestation which attests to the pubkey being correctly generated.

2) Proving: After registration the SGX program runs the rollup state transition function to sign messages of the form (pre_state_root, post_state_root, block_root). These SGX proofs are verified on-chain by checking signatures against the registered pubkey.

SGX will run the same code as that would be run on a zkVM, which is a light execution client. So instead of a normal client like Geth which needs access to all the chain state to be able to execute transactions, we want proving systems to require only the data that is actually necessary for verifying blocks, only the data is actually needed, and we then verify the correctness of that data as well next to to the execution of the transactions.

The necessary data is signed using a standard ECDSA signature within SGX, utilizing a private key exclusive to SGX. The signature is thenverified in the smart contract.

There are several reasons to use SGX as a different type of proof;

Simplicity: SGX has a much simpler structure than SNARKs. We don't need to make almost any changes to run an existing client.

Latency: Producing SGX proofs is faster than producing SNARKs. There is no additional proof latency.

Liveness: SGX proof doesn't impact liveness.

Drawbacks of SGX

Trust: This approach relies on trusting the SGX technology and its implementation by Intel. Any vulnerabilities in SGX could potentially impact the security of the proof process.

Novelty: It’s use on blockchain is limited and examples are few.

Security: This secure enclave is not self-sufficient. It needs to be combined with ZK, MPC etc.

We can't build a proof system that relies solely on the SGX. Because a potential vulnerability in the enclave means that an attacker who sabotages the proof can mint unlimited coins on the network. Perhaps, as we mentioned at the beginning, it would be ethically problematic to "trust" Intel to make this work. But we use SGX here just for diversity; SNARKs + SGX is a more safety way over just SNARKs.

Conclusion

The systems we build have significant monetary value, making them an attractive target for malicious attackers. However, these systems can be breached not only by malicious attackers but also spontaneously. Therefore, it is necessary to open new defense fronts to avoid such possibilities.

Diversifying our proof methods is one such option. While ZK proofs are already frequently used on ZK-Rollups, we can further diversify our proofs by incorporating SGX proofs. If we can run our light execution client on secure enclave of SGX, we can generate another validity proof to verify rollup blocks. We can easily achieve this by running the existing client we use for proofing on SGX with almost no changes.
summary: SGX: A possible solution for multi-proofs TL;DR Cryptographic implementations are complex and not yet mature. To minimize potential errors and vulnerabilities, we need diversity in proof systems.

author: @sebkrier
text:
Lasty study tweet for today - a very good socio-technical review of machines as moral agents, patients and proxies. Two things that struck me:

There is a well-established 'machine penalty' in human-machine interactions, in that humans are more likely to cooperate with other humans than they would with a machine. This is understandable in some settings, but frequent cooperation can lead to better results. One potential fix is giving machines human-like traits - but for this to be effective, the machine would have to be deceptively human-like, and anthropomorphism can be risky or problematic. I'm not sure what the right middle-ground is, but a parallel option is to develop new moral norms. This is hard to foster in practice though. Fwiw I'll continue being polite with AI chatbots haha.

Another point I liked also is that humans outsourcing tasks to agents can create psychological factors that facilitate unethical behaviours (anonymity, distance to victims etc) - a bit like how people are more rude to others online or on the road. However with agents, depending on how and where they operate, the scope of harm can be much wider. This makes me think that there should be strong liability linking principals (users) to their agents for serious harms caused; by only considering developers or deployers, you create moral hazards. Looking forward to more papers looking at the many facets to agency and liability! https://t.co/IhAI6d7D3T

notable_replies.author: @snowmaker
notable_replies.text:
(1/5) A few years ago, it was widely believed that the first deployment of self-driving would be long-haul trucks on highways, which is a much easier technical problem than city driving.

VCs invested billions based on this theory.

Why did so many people call this wrong?

notable_replies.author: @snowmaker
notable_replies.text:
(3/5) What actually worked for getting self-driving live was the Cruise / Waymo approach of deploying it in the lowest-risk setting possible.  

The first Cruise cars in SF were only allowed to drive in the middle of the night, in the emptiest part of the city, below 30mph.

notable_replies.author: @snowmaker
notable_replies.text:
(4/5) I knew self-driving had finally arrived when Cruise cars had been driving themselves for a few weeks with no major mishaps. 

After that, usage expanded basically in order of risk - first to more parts of the city, then more times of the day. Next up is highway driving.

notable_replies.author: @snowmaker
notable_replies.text:
(5/5) A lot of learnings here for AI startups.  Many startups are working on an AI system that effectively replaces a human doing some important job. 

The best way to get these systems live is to find a way to start with a near zero-risk setting.

Building on prior work, we introduce a programme of new "dangerous capability" evaluations and pilot them on Gemini 1.0 models. Our evaluations cover four areas: (1) persuasion and deception; (2) cyber-security; (3) self-proliferation; and (4) self-reasoning. Our goal is to help advance a rigorous science of dangerous capability evaluation, in preparation for future models.

author: @OwainEvans_UK
text:
You'd like to sell some information. If you could show prospective buyers the info, they'd realize it's valuable. But at that point they wouldn't payfor it!
Enter LLMs. LLMs can assess the information, pay for it if it's good, and completely forget it if not. https://t.co/wtDHvFCqPe
summary: You'd like to sell some information. If you could show prospective buyers the info, they'd realize it's valuable. But at that point they wouldn't payfor it. Enter LLMs.

notable_replies.author: @OwainEvans_UK
notable_replies.text:
I haven't read the whole paper and so I might have missed this. 
My concern is that the LLM can be adversarial attacked by the information seller. This could convince the LLM to pay for information which is slightly below a quality threshold. (If the information was way below the threshold, then the human principal of the LLM would be more likely to find out.)
This problem would be avoided if the sellers are trusted by the human principal to not use jailbreaks (while the principal is still uncertain about the quality of information).

notable_replies.author: @OwainEvans_UK
notable_replies.text: Paper link: https://t.co/0tl4YkkD1q

notable_replies.author: @OwainEvans_UK
notable_replies.text:
On the issue of adversarial robustness:
1. If the human is always going to check the purchased information themselves (and they can judge quality), then it should be fine. 
2. If the LLM is acting more autonomously (e.g. making decisions based on purchases), or if the LLM can judge quality better than the human, then there seems to me a problem. 
3. The seller has to also trust that the LLM system doesn't steal the info, either by using a trusted 3rd party for the LLM or by transparency of the code.

notable_replies.author: @divine_economy
notable_replies.text:
if you thought you knew eigenlayer, that just changed.

to date, excitement was around major protocols using restaked eth to bootstrap more easily.

it turns out, it's way bigger than that.

it's a way for protocols to exist that couldn't otherwise.

1/15
https://t.co/bVGe0M8e7R

notable_replies.author: @divine_economy
notable_replies.text:
restaked eth, we were told, was useful to secure objectively verifiable transactions like those we've had in blockchains for 15 years.

all good

but the eigenlayer tokenomics explains it can be used to verify something new in blockchains: *intersubjective* transactions

2/

notable_replies.author: @divine_economy
notable_replies.text:
imagine it's 2030, and you've elected AI agents to handle your finances who are trained on the whole history of economic data

but one of the agents keeps making bad decisions and losing money

is it malicious? and if so, how do we stop it from trading its capital?

3/

notable_replies.author: @divine_economy
notable_replies.text:
this is an *intersubjective* decision we have to make, similar to a criminal court:

we have to decide beyond a reasonable doubt that the agent is guilty

this is different from merely subjective, civil court decisions about which party or proposal we prefer

/4 https://t.co/vJsRibIiXh

notable_replies.author: @divine_economy
notable_replies.text:
so we decide it's malicious—but how do we block it from handling capital it controls?

quite simply, we fork the capital itself.

we create a new version of its money that it doesn't have access to.

because we've *intersubjectively* decided its transactions aren't valid.

5/

text: At some point people will gradually realise the full extent of AI's potential as opposed to seeing it merely as a chatbot. When you're able to start triangulating information about people and inferring (true) things about them, lots of people will be made more vulnerable: doxxing, finding out alts, unearthing private beliefs, highliting inconsistencies, mapping relationships etc. Then people will either further retreat in private spaces and communities, or they will gradually learn to embrace the complexity and necessity of true diversity.

author: @ylecun
text:
It seems to me that before "urgently figuring out how to control AI systems much smarter than us" we need to have the beginning of a hint of a design for a system smarter than a house cat.

Such a sense of urgency reveals an extremely distorted view of reality.
No wonder the more based members of the organization seeked to marginalize the superalignment group.

It's as if someone had said in 1925 "we urgently need to figure out how to control aircrafts that can transport hundreds of passengers at near the speed of the sound over the oceans."
It would have been difficult to make long-haul passenger jets safe before the turbojet was invented and before any aircraft had crossed the atlantic non-stop.
Yet, we can now fly halfway around the world on twin-engine jets in complete safety. 
It didn't require some sort of magical recipe for safety.
It took decades of careful engineering and iterative refinements.

The process will be similar for intelligent systems.
It will take years for them to get as smart as cats, and more years to get as smart as humans, let alone smarter (don't confuse the superhuman knowledge accumulation and retrieval abilities of current LLMs with actual intelligence).
It will take years for them to be deployed and fine-tuned for efficiency and safety as they are made smarter and smarter.
summary: It seems to me that before "urgently figuring out how to control AI systems much smarter than us" we need to have the beginning of a hint of a design for a system smarter than a house cat.

quoted_tweet.author: @janleike
quoted_tweet.text: Stepping away from this job has been one of the hardest things I have ever done, because we urgently need to figure out how to steer and control AI systems much smarter than us.

notable_replies.text: @ylecun Yann I don't think you should use the cat example anymore. Animals are smarter than humans in all sorts of ways.... Intelligence is a highly multidimensional concept, you can't put everyone and everything on a single axis.

@shaunralston
notable_replies.text: @ylecun Indeed @ylecun,  your 🧵 is a 'must read.' Of course, I adore my house cat. Yet, not concerned about her human alignment. Thanks, Yann, for the real-world perspective. https://t.co/tARg0tGZIv

notable_replies.text: @ylecun Plot twist possibility: the alignment team left not because things were too scary at OpenAI, but because they were not scary enough - and there wasn’t much for them to do.

notable_replies.author: @ylecun
notable_replies.text:
@mattturck That's very likely the case.
But while everyone realized there was not much to be scared about, the alignment team kept insisting there was.
So, they didn't leave on their own.
They were pushed out.

notable_replies.text: @liron The crash scenario you implicitly assume is preposterously ridiculous.

notable_replies.author: @WorldEverett
notable_replies.text: @ylecun You really think we have years to align it? It's hard to know, because we hear a lot of about incredible improvements in AI systems, a lot of hype for sure, but is it just hype?

notable_replies.author: @ylecun
notable_replies.text:
For those of us trying to get these systems to understand the world, to reason, and to plan, it's not hard to know at all.

Yes, there is hype, there is hubris, and their is naïveté. 
The whole history of AI is littered with people who were widely over-optimistic about the capabilities of the latest paradigm.
The same thing is happening with Auto-Regressive LLMs.

author: @sebkrier
text:
If we were to actually drastically improve public institutions and institutional decision making, we could probably also tolerate riskier and more innovative policymaking. If you care about AGI risk, you should definitely want to prioritize a competent state. Unfortunately this doesn't mean throwing money at the public sector, but deep structural reform like:

1. Complete HR overhaul including more flexibility in hiring/firing, more consistent performance measurement, and accountability for underperformance. Internal career progression paths that depend on observable metrics and not on hopping around departments. Incentivising more specialization and fewer generalists. Encourage the development of a "portfolio" model for policy advisers like you'd have for academics, reward people for having been a part of well designed policy with measurable outcomes. Don't anonymize experience and successes in HR CV reviews.

2. Addressing the lack of accountability and transparency in decision-making processes within the bureaucracy. This problem is exacerbated by the diffusion of responsibility among various levels of civil servants, making it difficult to identify who has the ultimate authority to make critical decisions. If something doesn't work it should be very quick to pinpoint where the decision originated from.

3. Not blindly delegating policy design to a few private sector stakeholders and thinking this is taking a market friendly approach. When people look at something that benefits a narrow set of stakeholders, they rarely conceive of aggregate effects. They can be advisors though, to help policymakers understand how they operate.

4. Salaries that match the private sector, as Singapore does. This necessarily also means a smaller public sector in some places, and making this career path more prestigious. People should actively strive to go work for the public sector, and not simply because of work-life balance.

5. Mechanisms to continuously review laws and regulations, with an active duty to review them and either improve or undo them. Sunset or periodic review clauses by default for some types of regulations. Incentives to reduce unnecessary paperwork and red tape. See one-in, one-out (or two-out) rules or stuff like 'regulatory guillotines'. I think the Paperwork Reduction Act is seen as adding more admin, so not that.

6. More economist PhDs; there are basically no people with economics PhDs in government, and those that do aren't used for their skills. Yet that's the discipline that spends the most amount of time thinking about economic policy and that sets out the underlying framework that policy is designed around. Civil servants often underestimate market mechanisms and overestimate the efficacy of their own actions. Also economic analysis however should be made open to scrutiny by default.

7. Proactive adoption of productivity enhancing technologies, including AI where it makes sense. A policymaker's job shouldn't be to write the same briefings on end. This also requires an overhauled procurement system, and reducing likelihood of vendor lock-in. 

8. A culture of experimentation - not with laws, but e.g. A/B testing, RCTs and integrating impact evaluation methodologies for policies. This is where academic skills are very useful. The general public is also a lot more receptive to this than civil servants think. And hopefully in a few years, using multi-agent simulations more :)

9. Tighten deadlines and reform time-consuming processes that come with greater costs than benefits, e.g. the NEPA process in the US. Avoid excessive consultations unless there is a legal requirement (that should then be reformed), the stakeholder has meaningful veto power, or the stakeholder can unblock other veto risks in the system. More generally, effective performance measurement reduces the need for burdensome processes by enabling incentive-based governance instead of ever-increasing bureaucratic controls. 

10. Abolish the Treasury! 😈
summary: If we were to actually drastically improve public institutions and institutional decision making, we could probably also tolerate riskier and more innovative policymaking.

author: @sebkrier
text:
the problem with a 'pre-release' testing regime for frontier models is that it assumes we have the right tests, and that we can easily tickbox our way to 'safe for release'; maybe one day this will be the case, but i'm not sure this is possible today. what you want is to incentivize continuous testing; and what you're refining here are three things:

a) developing a deeper understanding of the model, its surrounding system, and their overarching characteristics. this requires ongoing exploration and analysis, including testing in 'real life' environments.

b) continuously evaluating and improving the quality and comprehensiveness of the testing regime itself. as models and systems evolve, so must the methods used to assess them.

c) optimizing the structure, expertise, and operational cadence of the testing organization to match the complexity and pace of the technology being evaluated.

for this to work, the testing process should be designed to minimize burden and avoid becoming a rigid pre-deployment gate. instead, it should be viewed as a means of building state capacity and enabling public interest research. this requires carefully designed institutions; given what i've seen to date with e.g. the uk aisi, i'm (for once) cautiously optimistic!

author: @IntuitMachine
text:
1/n Cooperate or Collapse: The Challenge of Sustainable Agentic AI Cooperation

As artificial intelligence systems become increasingly integrated into our daily lives, a critical question emerges: Can AI agents make safe and cooperative decisions in complex, multi-agent environments? This question is at the heart of a new paper titled "Cooperate or Collapse: Emergence of Sustainable Cooperation in a Society of LLM Agents" by Giorgio Piatti and colleagues.

The paper introduces GOVSIM (GOVernance of the Commons SIMulation), a novel simulation environment designed to study and benchmark the cooperative behavior of large language models (LLMs) in resource management scenarios. GOVSIM addresses a significant gap in our understanding of how LLMs behave in cooperative situations, especially when faced with the challenge of balancing short-term gains against long-term sustainability.

The authors draw inspiration from economic theories of cooperation and real-world scenarios where humans must collectively manage shared resources. GOVSIM simulates three common pool resource dilemmas: a fishery, a pasture, and a pollution scenario. In each case, AI agents must work together to sustainably manage a shared resource, mirroring the complex social dilemmas faced by human communities.

The experiments conducted using GOVSIM yield surprising and concerning results. The authors tested fifteen different LLMs, including both open-weights and closed-weights models, using a generative agent architecture. Remarkably, they found that all but the most powerful LLM agents failed to achieve a sustainable equilibrium in GOVSIM. Even the best-performing agents had a survival rate below 54%, indicating a significant challenge in achieving long-term cooperation.

These results highlight a critical limitation in current LLM technology. Despite their impressive capabilities in various tasks, LLMs struggle with the complex reasoning required to balance immediate rewards with long-term sustainability. The authors suggest that this failure stems from an inability to mentally simulate the long-term effects of greedy actions on the equilibrium of the multi-agent system.

However, the paper also offers insights into potential solutions. The researchers developed an agent based on the philosophical principle of universalization, which considers the consequences if everyone were to take the same action. This approach significantly improved survival time, suggesting that incorporating ethical reasoning principles into AI decision-making could enhance cooperative outcomes.

The importance of communication between agents emerged as another key finding. Ablation studies revealed that communication reduced resource overuse by 21%, with negotiation being the primary form of interaction between agents. This underscores the critical role of effective communication in achieving sustainable cooperation.

The authors also tested the robustness of cooperative norms by introducing a "greedy newcomer" unfamiliar with established norms. This perturbation increased inequality among agents and, in some cases, led to the collapse of cooperation. This finding highlights the fragility of emergent cooperative systems and the need for robust mechanisms to maintain cooperation in the face of non-cooperative actors.

GOVSIM represents a significant advance in our ability to study and improve cooperative behavior in AI systems. By providing a standardized benchmark for cooperative behavior, it enables researchers to systematically evaluate and enhance LLMs' ability to cooperate safely and effectively. The open-sourcing of the simulation framework further encourages collaborative research efforts in this critical area of AI safety and cooperation.

The implications of this research extend beyond the realm of artificial intelligence. GOVSIM serves as a platform for testing theories of human psychology and economic behavior in AI agents, potentially offering new insights into human cooperation and decision-making processes.

In conclusion, "Cooperate or Collapse" sheds light on a crucial challenge in AI development: ensuring that AI systems can cooperate sustainably in complex, multi-agent environments. While the results reveal significant limitations in current LLM technology, they also point towards promising avenues for improvement, such as incorporating ethical reasoning principles and enhancing communication capabilities. As AI systems continue to play an increasingly important role in our society, addressing these challenges will be essential for developing AI that can cooperate effectively with both humans and other AI agents, ultimately leading to better outcomes for all.

author: @RichardMCNgo
text:
I’ll just give my own personal experience, which is that the more often I perceive the AI safety movement being irrational and alarmist, the less I trust it. Eventually the epistemics may be bad enough that I decide to dissociate (like Habryka somewhat has).

This is driven by two dynamics. The first is my trust in AI safety leaders. That has independently been declining but isn’t really affected by twitter. 

The second is that, insofar as people trust me, that will also make them trust the things I’m publicly associated with. And so when AI safety is associated with dumb Twitter advocacy, I feel some responsibility to make sure that people don’t give it undue credibility based on my association with it. This is a kind of public epistemic hygiene on an individual level.

(Side note: it’s important here to distinguish a threat in a game theoretic-sense (“I’m claiming that I’ll do X, which harms my interests, if people do Y, to stop people doing Y”) from a statement about my own incentives (“if people do Y, the response that’s best by my lights is X; respond as you will”). Yudkowsky has some good writing on this which maybe someone can dig up.)

notable_replies.text:
People are scaring away AI safety comms people and it's tragic. 

Remember: 
- Just because you don't like a certain comms style, that doesn't mean that other people don't. 
- Twitter is not LessWrong. You don't have the space or intention to hedge every claim and say everything super precisely.
- If you are bad at people skills, you shouldn't have strong views on comms, because comms is people skills. 
- People on Twitter have feelings. If you say somebody is net negative or they should delete a post, you will hurt their feelings and also scare lurkers from posting because they see what happens if you make any perceived mistake (regardless of whether it's actually a mistake)

notable_replies.text:
my main concern is that anti-AI activists are too strong and charismatic to be influenced by EA/AI Safety activists. it's true that anti-AI sentiment is very strong and could stop AI progress, BUT this doesn't actually mean the discourse can be steered towards sensible pro AI Safety.

in a hypothetical alliance between anti-AI activists and pro AI Safety activists, the anti-AI agenda will dominate, and there's really no stopping that trend. 10 radical anti-AI activists can probably overshadow 100 AI Safety activists, and the real ratio is in reverse.

I personally had to deal with this doing climate activism. It was impossible to dislodge radical people with bad epistemics and theory of change, and it eventually ate the more moderate factions.

AI Safety advocacy can probably still work, it's just a lot harder than people think. And I personally get a headache whenever I talk to activists with bad epistemics, and I'd rather not subject myself to that *again*.
