notable_replies.author: @atroyn
notable_replies.text:
i spent the weekend working to try to get more data about the question of whether or not gpt has world models

my results seem to suggest it doesn't, but i found some interesting things along the way. writeup below.

notable_replies.author: @atroyn
notable_replies.text:
the entire question really kicked off for me when people were using gpt's performance on chess under certain conditions as strong evidence for the idea that it has world models

at the same time, it couldn't play well from random positions

https://t.co/WKwikUSo9v

notable_replies.author: @atroyn
notable_replies.text: the claim that gpt played chess well because it has a world model of chess is a very very strong claim, which entails that gpt knows the rules of chess, can consistently apply them, and knows good strategy

notable_replies.author: @atroyn
notable_replies.text: the explanation that it plays badly when presented with random positions is because it can also model bad play is an even stronger claim

notable_replies.author: @atroyn
notable_replies.text:
game of life does not have 'good' and 'bad' play - only application of the rules correctly and consistently

explanations and examples of game of life definitely appear in gpt's training data, but it would be very rare for any given 10x10 board to appear at all

notable_replies.author: @atroyn
notable_replies.text: additionally, game of life's statistics are unbalanced; of 512 possible 9-element neighborhoods, only 140 produce a live cell at the next iteration (27%)

notable_replies.author: @atroyn

author: @Simeon_Cps
text:
Wild times. The UK government might be the adult in the room against AI extinction risks.

Former adviser to Prime Minister nailed it in his article, through 3 core points: 

1. We need compute thresholds back on the table until we're actually capable of demonstrating safety. 

2. We need to develop algorithms that are bounded. S. Russell, J. Tenenbaum's MIT group, ARIA's @davidad or @ConjectureAI are all working on that but we need 10x as much resources/talent going into this. 

3. We need commitments not to release next generation of models before they've tested and vetted by democratically accountable bodies. I'd just replace "release" by "train" but both are great. 

There's a lot of interest to actually pursue ambitious & sane policies. We're all gonna make it.

quoted_tweet.author: @AnEmergentI
quoted_tweet.text:
I've got a short piece in today's Spectator (need to sign up to read). Key point: AI companies cannot be allowed to mark their own homework. 
https://t.co/dXYCDxfE6p

Points made:
- When in No10 our team got increasingly concerned that behind scenes, frontier AI companies thought they may be much closer to creating AGI-type tech than publicly recognised/official advisory channels said, and some were v concerned about where we would be in 5 years time.
- AI safety summit is occurring to begin international dialogue on these frontier risks.
- It is v challenging to forsee specific risks of an unbounded, highly intelligent system.  This isn't well recognised.
-This year, public statements from ppl whose estimates of tech trajectory have been most correct, like Hassabis +Shane Legg, have placed AGI as likely within this decade. They may be wrong, but they have been most right.
- Companies stuck in a race, despite acknowledgement of major risks.
- Already, AI is showing specific worrisome capabilities in chemical/bioweaponry.
-As systems approach and surpass superintelligence, this will only grow and diversify in risk.
-If u went back in time, ppl would likely say 'be v cautious about this', but now we are here if anything race is accelerating with ever increasing capital going into it.
- Govt has made an AI Taskforce to approach this, but this has harder task than the vaccine effort as there isn't the global recognition or consensus there was around vaccines.
- Tech companies are currently pushing 'evals', but whilst useful this doesn't meaningfully create  independent checks and controls on the techs progress.
- We need commitments not to release next generation of models until they have been security tested by democratically accountable bodies.
- Political paralysis in US means we are dependent on goodwill from tech companies, and this risks regulatory capture by Big Tech.
- Incentives align with creating unbounded, hard to interpret algorithms. Need international lab to push independent testing, development of algorithms that are bounded. Some progress on this but not enough. 
- Measures like compute caps are off table, need to be back on table at least for a while whilst world orients to this moment.
- Just getting a summit is a good achievement, but going forward we need to go much further and not let a few companies control this moment in history.
https://t.co/dXYCDxfE6p

quoted_tweet.text:
I've got some bad news for everyone.

If we try to control superintelligence with government - and we do it in a competitive marketplace of companies and nations - it will end with the superintelligence controlling our government. 

Governments, companies, nations, regulators etc leak power like crazy. Democracy leaks power because voters can be controlled via propaganda, intimidation and immigration. 

It's my view that all winning states factor through finding automated governance mechanisms that are capable of actually controlling that much power. 

A good analogy is that if you load enough voltage onto a pair of metal cables separated by an airgap, eventually the air breaks down and arcs. Trying to control superintelligence using human institutions will go the same way: Moore's Law will turn the power up over time, and eventually it will just break out institutions. 

A mini-version of this already happened with social media feeding back into democratic processes from about 2010 onwards.

text:
> we won't be able to tell if they're being deceptive

I think this is very likely false. Three main reasons:
1. NNs are differentiable functions so you can look at the logits to detect hesitations or anomalies that may not be obvious in the actual text/actions that are sampled; Owain's work demonstrates this
2. We have full white box access to the model and can throw countless anomaly detection tools at all its internals; I personally have shown this can be used to detect prompt injection attacks
3. We will have a wide array of narrow superhuman AIs that can help us with evaluation and interrogation of the AIs we're most worried about  https://t.co/XUqgZPOoIu

notable_replies.text:
Pressure Testing GPT-4-128K With Long Context Recall

128K tokens of context is awesome - but what's performance like?

I wanted to find out so I did a “needle in a haystack” analysis

Some expected (and unexpected) results

Here's what I found:

Findings:
* GPT-4’s recall performance started to degrade above 73K tokens
* Low recall performance was correlated when the fact to be recalled was placed between at 7%-50% document depth
* If the fact was at the beginning of the document, it was recalled regardless of context length

So what:
* No Guarantees - Your facts are not guaranteed to be retrieved. Don’t bake the assumption they will into your applications
* Less context = more accuracy - This is well know, but when possible reduce the amount of context you send to GPT-4 to increase its ability to recall
* Position matters - Also well know, but facts placed at the very beginning and 2nd half of the document seem to be recalled better

Overview of the process:
* Use Paul Graham essays as ‘background’ tokens. With 218 essays it’s easy to get up to 128K tokens
* Place a random statement within the document at various depths. Fact used: “The best thing to do in San Francisco is eat a sandwich and sit in Dolores Park on a sunny day.”
* Ask GPT-4 to answer this question only using the context provided
* Evaluate GPT-4s answer with another model (gpt-4 again) using @langchain evals
* Rinse and repeat for 15x document depths between 0% (top of document) and 100% (bottom of document) and 15x context lengths (1K Tokens > 128K Tokens)

Next Steps To Take This Further:
* Iterations of this analysis were evenly distributed, it’s been suggested that doing a sigmoid distribution would be better (it would tease out more nuanced at the start and end of the document)
* For rigor, one should do a key:value retrieval step. However for relatability I did a San Francisco line within PGs essays.

Notes:
* While I think this will be directionally correct, more testing is needed to get a firmer grip on GPT4s abilities
* Switching up prompt with vary results
* 2x tests were run at large context lengths to tease out more performance
* This test cost ~$200 for API calls (a single call at 128K input tokens costs $1.28)
* Thank you to @charles_irl for being a sounding board and providing great next steps

summary: 🧵Announcing GPQA, a graduate-level “Google-proof” Q&A benchmark designed for scalable oversight.

notable_replies.author: @idavidrein
notable_replies.text: It contains 448 questions written by experts in biology, chemistry, and physics. When attempting questions out of their own domain (e.g., a physicist answers a chemistry question), these experts get only 34% accuracy, despite spending >30m with full access to Google. https://t.co/hX7Usu3Uyo

notable_replies.author: @idavidrein
notable_replies.text: The questions are also high-quality: experts within the same domain have a 74% agreement rate when discounting clear mistakes the experts identified in retrospect, and post-hoc they agree with the given answers on 85% of the questions. https://t.co/MF1nmKMRHy

notable_replies.author: @idavidrein
notable_replies.text: Proposed scalable oversight methods like debate need high-quality evaluation testbeds to measure results. GPQA is hard enough to measure differences between oversight methods that we expect can generalize to questions no human can currently answer (fig: https://t.co/DuCS1AT1uc). https://t.co/dCMdZO2l4H

author: @sog_on_bird_app
text:
Now combine Q learning + A* + LLMs

Conceptual Integration

-Defining States and Actions:
 States: Each token or a sequence of tokens during the generation of text.

-Actions: The choice of the next token or sequence of tokens.

-Applying Q-Learning:

 Develop a reward function for the LM, where desirable responses (e.g., coherent, relevant answers) are rewarded.

-Use Q-learning to learn the Q-values for state-action pairs (token sequences and response choices).

-Incorporating A Search*:

-The heuristic in A* could estimate the 'cost' to reach a desirable output (e.g., a coherent, complete answer) from the current state (current token sequence).

-This heuristic needs to be defined in the context of language generation, such as estimating the distance from the current state to a state that represents a high-quality, complete response.

-Combining A with Q-Values for
Multi-Turn Reasoning*:

-In a multi-turn conversation, the goal is to optimize not just the immediate response but the entire sequence of interactions.

-The A* algorithm could be applied to traverse the 'graph' of possible token sequences, using Q-values as part of its heuristic. This means that the path chosen by A* not only seeks to minimize the estimated cost to reach a high-quality response but also considers the learned Q-values which reflect the cumulative reward of getting there.

-Optimizing the Process:
 Store and reuse Q-values and heuristic estimations for similar states in future interactions, speeding up the decision-making process.

-Continuously update the Q-values and heuristics based on feedback and new data.
summary: Now combine Q learning + A* + LLMs Conceptual Integration -Defining States and Actions: States: Each token or a sequence of tokens during the generation of text.

notable_replies.author: @sog_on_bird_app
notable_replies.text:
Then I used this nifty plugin on chatgpt called "Show Me" to ask it to explain it to me visually.

- The Player explores the maze and chooses actions.

- The Maze (Environment) provides the current state and reward to the player.

 - The Player checks the Q-Table (Guidebook) for Q-values associated with the current state.

 - The Q-Table suggests the best action to the Decision Making process.

 - The Decision Making process advises the player on which action to choose based on Q-values.

 - The Player performs the action in the environment.

 - The Environment updates the player with the new state and reward.

- The Player then updates the Q-Table with this new information.
 The Q-Table adjusts its Q-values accordingly.

- This process repeats each game iteration, with the player continuously exploring and the Q-Table updating, leading to improved strategies over time.

notable_replies.author: @sog_on_bird_app
notable_replies.text:
Now I asked it to explain A star search.

Alright, imagine you're playing a video game where you're on a quest to find treasure. You're in a big maze with lots of paths, and you want to find the quickest way to the treasure without wandering around too much.

The A* (pronounced "A-star") search algorithm is like a super smart guide in this game. It helps you find the fastest path to the treasure.

Here's how it works:
 Starting Point: You begin at the start of the maze.
 Looking Around: At each point in the maze, you look at all the paths you can take next.
 Smart Guessing: For each path, A* makes a smart guess about how close it will get you to the treasure. It's like it's saying, "Hmm, if you go this way, it looks like you'll be this close to the treasure."
 Picking the Best Path: Out of all these guesses, A* picks the path that seems like it'll get you closest to the treasure the fastest.
 Repeating: You keep doing this - moving forward, looking at paths, making smart guesses - until you find the treasure.

The cool part about A* is that it's really good at guessing which way is best. It uses a special formula to make these guesses, combining how far you've already traveled and how far it thinks you still have to go.

So, A* is like having a really clever friend in the game who helps you find the best way through the maze, saving you time and getting you to the treasure quickly!

notable_replies.author: @sog_on_bird_app
notable_replies.text:
-Starting Point: It begins at where you are in the maze.

-Costs:
It knows the exact steps you've taken so far.

It also makes a smart guess about how many steps it might take to reach the end from where you are now.

-Best Path Calculation: It adds these two numbers (steps taken + steps guessed) to figure out which path might be the quickest.

-Looking Around:
It keeps track of the places it has checked and the places it still needs to check.
It always picks the next place to check based on which one looks like it might have the shortest total path.

-Exploring: It goes around the maze, looking at all the paths from the current spot and updating its guesses about the quickest path.

-Finding the Path: If it reaches the end of the maze, it shows you the path it found. If it finds out there's no way to the end, it tells you that too.

-The End: The game ends either when you reach the end of the maze or if the helper has checked everywhere and can't find a way through.

author: @pmarca
text: You literally want to use the threat of government force to stop me from doing certain kinds of computations because of your half baked pet theory built on an edifice of independent abstract arguments.
summary: You literally want to use the threat of government force to stop me from doing certain kinds of computations because of your half baked pet theory built on an edifice of independent abstract arguments...

quoted_tweet.author: @RatOrthodox
quoted_tweet.text:
I have a lot of sympathy for a certain kind of objection to my worldview. To summarize:

"You literally want to use the threat of government force to stop me from doing certain kinds of computations because of your half baked pet theory built on an edifice of independent abstract arguments. These computations are extremely useful and benefit many people btw!"

I have a lot of sympathy for this type of objection. I don't look down on anyone for making this kind of objection. In nearby worlds I would have been right there alongside you.

And yet, I still think that very probably the wise move for humanity would be to unprecedentedly slow down frontier ML research. This is not because I am insensitive to the kind of argument I summarize above, but because I am sensitive to a different kind of argument about the extreme power of general intelligence, and the extreme difficulty of getting this particular engineering problem right. It is possible and I think a sign of good conscience to be sensitive to both of these kinds of reasons simultaneously.  

I guess I wanted to make it clear that if my summary rhymes with your primary objection, we are really not so different, and there are probably many mutually beneficial conversations left for us to have.

linked_content.abstract: Typical deep visual recognition models are capable of performing the one task they were trained on. In this paper, we tackle the extremely difficult problem of combining distinct models with different initializations, each solving a separate task, into one multi-task model without any additional training. Prior work in model merging permutes one model to the space of the other then averages them together. While this works for models trained on the same task, we find that this fails to account for the differences in models trained on disjoint tasks. Thus, we introduce "ZipIt!", a general method for merging two arbitrary models of the same architecture that incorporates two simple strategies. author: @DrJimFan
text:
Today is the beginning of our moonshot to solve embodied AGI in the physical world. I’m so excited to announce Project GR00T, our new initiative to create a general-purpose foundation model for humanoid robot learning.

The GR00T model will enable a robot to understand multimodal instructions, such as language, video, and demonstration, and perform a variety of useful tasks. We are collaborating with many leading humanoid companies around the world, so that GR00T may transfer across embodiments and help the ecosystem thrive.

GR00T is born on NVIDIA’s deep technology stack. We simulate in Isaac Lab (new app on Omniverse Isaac Sim for humanoid learning), train on OSMO (new compute orchestration system to scale up models), and deploy to Jetson Thor (new edge GPU chip designed to power GR00T).

Announced in Jensen's keynote, Project GR00T is a cornerstone for the “Foundation Agent” roadmap of the newly founded GEAR Lab. At GEAR, we are building generally capable agents that learn to act skillfully in many worlds, virtual and real. See if you can spot "GEAR" in the video ;)

Join us on the journey to land on the moon.
summary: Today is the beginning of our moonshot to solve embodied AGI in the physical world.

author: @Scott_Wiener
text:
AI policy is a new & fast-moving field & it’s healthy & important to have a diversity of perspectives. 

However, this thread contains some extreme inaccuracies — indeed outright fear-mongering — about our AI safety legislation (SB 1047) that need to be corrected: 🧵
summary: AI policy is a new & fast-moving field & it’s healthy & important to have a diversity of perspectives.

quoted_tweet.author: @brianchau57
quoted_tweet.text:
The California senate bill to crush OpenAI's competitors is fast tracked for a vote. This is the most brazen attempt to hurt startups and open source yet.

🧵 https://t.co/VXIwvq7LiH

notable_replies.author: @Scott_Wiener
notable_replies.text: 1️⃣ SB 1047 is meticulously designed to set robust & attainable safety standards for frontier model developers. We’ve worked intensively w/ the startup community & have support of startups like @imbue_ai. We’ve advanced this framework b/c innovators like imbue say it’s workable.

notable_replies.author: @Scott_Wiener
notable_replies.text:
This support goes beyond businesses like Imbue, Lovable Labs, other startups and business groups like the @laareachamber. 

We’ve gotten support from the godfathers of AI @geoffreyhinton & Yoshua Bengio, who have been leading innovators in this space for over 4 decades.

notable_replies.author: @Scott_Wiener
notable_replies.text:
2️⃣ The idea that SB 1047 would “make it a felony to make a paperwork mistake for this agency” is false & not how liability works.

The bill only allows criminal penalties for perjury, which requires a jury to convict someone for intentionally lying in writing to the government.

notable_replies.author: @QuintinPope5
notable_replies.text:
Thank you @Scott_Wiener for providing your perspective on the bill's intent. I'd appreciate it if you directly address the specific scenario Brain raises at the end of his thread.

Suppose an open model developer releases an innocuous email writing model, and fraudsters then attach malware to the emails written by that model. Are the model developers then potentially liable for the fraudsters' malfeasance under the derivative model clause?

notable_replies.author: @krishnanrohit
notable_replies.text: @Scott_Wiener Senator, if someone creates a ransomware that causes a billion dollars of damage using Microsoft visual studio, are you going to be suing the developers of Microsoft visual studio?

notable_replies.author: @delk
notable_replies.text:
@Scott_Wiener AI is SF and CA's best hope for financial abundance (and national relevance) for the next decade. Passing the most aggressive regulations in the country for the industry most likely to save the state is a baffling choice. 

AGI is not around the corner, wait and get this right.

author: @swyx
text:
IMO @AnthropicAI is very close to making a breakthrough in productizable interpretability.

For ~4 years all we've had to really control LLMs is temperature/top_p and logit bias. We recently got `seed` and constrained structured output, with `interactive=false` on the way.

But now Claude Sonnet can let people clamp up/down 34 million features ranging from famous people and noun categories to abstract concepts like its ability to keep a secret, code errors (!) and its representation of self. This is "representation engineering writ large", and probably easy to retrain the SAEs for any set of features you care about.

Do not sleep on their paper. Ground breaking series of work that led up to today.
summary: IMO @AnthropicAI is very close to making a breakthrough in productizable interpretability. For ~4 years all we've had to really control LLMs is temperature/top_p and logit bias.

quoted_tweet.author: @thesephist
quoted_tweet.text:
By end of 2024, steering foundation models in latent/activation space will outperform steering in token space ("prompt eng") in several large production deployments.

I felt skeptical about this in summer '23, felt vaguely positive in Jan, and now think it's more likely than not, and I'm more optimistic than ever about the direction of my work since 2022 around a joint exploration of interfaces and latent visualization/steering of foundation models. Anthro's published work today is a milestone in a steady march toward this future that started in mid 2023.

Anthropic and DM's leadership in this area, combined with lots of community efforts in work like steering vectors, better sparse autoencoders, various image editing UI prototypes all push us toward the future here, but once technical foundations are there, interface will be much more obviously a bottleneck to utility, alignment, and capability.

I'm very excited about the interface possibilities this will open up, particularly for multimodal models and creative use cases. For a moment I thought it was possible that dialogue may eat everything. I don't think so anymore. We'll see new universes of possibilities in both.

(And if frontier labs don't have serious interface research bets today, this would probably be a good time to reconsider it :-)

author: @karpathy
text:
Nice, a serious contender to @lmsysorg in evaluating LLMs has entered the chat.

LLM evals are improving, but not so long ago their state was very bleak, with qualitative experience very often disagreeing with quantitative rankings.

This is because good evals are very difficult to build - at Tesla I probably spent 1/3 of my time on data, 1/3 on evals, and 1/3 on everything else. They have to be comprehensive, representative, of high quality, and measure gradient signal (i.e. not too easy, not too hard), and there are a lot of details to think through and get right before your qualitative and quantitative assessments line up. My goto pointer for some of the fun subtleties is probably the Open LLM Leaderboard MMLU writeup: https://t.co/Ns1hfEct4k

The other non-obvious part is that any open (non-private) test dataset inevitably leak into training sets. This is something people strongly intuitively suspect, and also why this GSM1k made rounds recently
https://t.co/0jzJNb2SXK

Even if LLM developers do their best, preventing test sets from seeping into training sets (and answers getting memorized) is difficult. Sure, you can do your best to filter out exact matches. You can also filter out approximate matches with n-gram overlaps or so. But how do you filter out synthetic data re-writes, or related online discussions about the data? Once we start routinely training multi-modal models, how do you filter out images/screenshots of the data? How do you prevent developers from e.g. vector embedding the test sets, and specifically targeting training todata that has high alignment (in the embedding space) with the test sets?

And the last component of this is that not all LLM tasks we care about are automatically evaluateable (e.g. think summarization, etc), and at that point you want to involve humans. And when you do, how do you control for all the variables involved, e.g. how much people pay attention to the actual answer, or the length, or the style, or how refusals are treated, etc.

Anyway, good evals are unintuitively difficult, highly work-intensive, but quite important, so I'm happy to see more organizations join the effort to do it well.

notable_replies.author: @JacobHHilton
notable_replies.text: When I left @OpenAI a little over a year ago, I signed a non-disparagement agreement, with non-disclosure about the agreement itself, for no other reason than to avoid losing my vested equity. (Thread)

notable_replies.author: @JacobHHilton
notable_replies.text: The agreement was unambiguous that in return for signing, I was being allowed to keep my vested equity, and offered nothing more. I do not see why anyone would have signed it if they had thought it would have no impact on their equity.

notable_replies.author: @JacobHHilton
notable_replies.text: I left OpenAI on great terms, so I assume this agreement was imposed upon almost all departing employees. I had no intention to criticize OpenAI before I signed the agreement, but was nevertheless disappointed to give up my right to do so.

notable_replies.author: @JacobHHilton
notable_replies.text: Yesterday, OpenAI reached out to me to release me from this agreement, following @KelseyTuoc's excellent investigative reporting.

notable_replies.author: @JacobHHilton
notable_replies.text: First among those is a binding commitment to non-retaliation. Even now, OpenAI can prevent employees from selling their equity, rendering it effectively worthless for an unknown period of time.

notable_replies.author: @JacobHHilton
notable_replies.text: In a statement, OpenAI has said, "Historically, former employees have been eligible to sell at the same price regardless of where they work; we don’t expect that to change."

notable_replies.author: @JacobHHilton
notable_replies.text: I believe that OpenAI has honest intentions with this statement. But given that OpenAI has previously used access to liquidity as an intimidation tactic, many former employees will still feel scared to speak out.

author: @joeykrug
text: If you spend $10bb to train a model, you can’t give it away for free. Our investment in Sentient aims to change this dynamic. They’re trying to create cryptography embedded within lIms, so if you don't pay the model you can't use it. They call this “model loyalty.”
summary: If you spend $10bb to train a model, you can’t give it away for free. Our investment in Sentient aims to change this dynamic.

notable_replies.author: @joeykrug
notable_replies.text: We recently invested in #Sentient. It’s mostly an investment in the team for us, but there are also some interesting threads related to open vs closed source AI that I want to cover as to why we invested. More below:

notable_replies.author: @joeykrug
notable_replies.text: I’ve known Pramod and Sandeep for years, they’re both super sharp technologists and people I wouldn’t bet against. Pramod did a lot of early work on wireless networks, and also has published a bunch of novel papers (on scaling, networking, etc) in the crypto space. Sandeep I first met when we were looking at Matic (now Polygon) back in the Augur days. I’m excited to see him lead Sentient

notable_replies.author: @joeykrug
notable_replies.text: One of the great things about Founders Fund is our partners and founders we invest in can have divergent views, and we actually welcome that! John on our team recently published a piece on open source AI.

notable_replies.author: @joeykrug
notable_replies.text: While I believe the pros of open source (even natsec adjusted) outweigh the cons, I agree with the core of John's take that the economics of open source Al don’t make any sense whatsoever today. Capex heavy software is very different than low capex traditional software

notable_replies.author: @joeykrug
notable_replies.text: That way the model can still be open source, but it’s not actually usable without payment. It’d be possible to ship an MVP of this using Nvidia’s recent TEE trusted hardware. The rough mental model is Ethereum is open source, but it's not free to use, or something like DRM

notable_replies.author: @joeykrug
notable_replies.text: It’s definitely a big research challenge, but if they solve it, it could actually make it possible to monetize open source AI models.

notable_replies.author: @joeykrug
notable_replies.text: (And if you can monetize them, capitalist incentives will likely drive much stronger/smarter open source models than can exist under the current paradigm)

author: @SmokeAwayyy
text:
Level 6 (Global Coordinators):

At this level, AI systems go beyond managing single organizations to coordinate multiple organizations, industries, or even entire economies on a global scale. This involves a transition from organizational optimization to large-scale, cross-domain integration and decision-making. The key technical advancements here include:

1. Global Optimization: The AI must possess algorithms capable of optimizing resource allocation, supply chains, and economic strategies across multiple organizations and industries, considering global variables and constraints.

2. Multi-Domain Integration: AI systems need to integrate and process data from diverse fields such as economics, environmental science, public health, and international relations to make informed decisions that benefit global systems.

3. Policy Formulation and Implementation: Developing AI-driven tools that can formulate policies, predict their outcomes, and implement them effectively at an international level, considering the socio-economic and political impacts.

4. Real-Time Global Monitoring: Utilizing a network of sensors, satellites, and IoT devices to monitor global activities in real time, providing data for dynamic decision-making and rapid response to global events and crises.

5. Ethical Global Governance: Establishing frameworks for ethical governance on a global scale, ensuring that AI-driven decisions are equitable, transparent, and aligned with the values of diverse cultures and societies.
summary: Level 6 (Global Coordinators): At this level, AI systems go beyond managing single organizations to coordinate multiple organizations, industries, or even entire economies on a global scale.

notable_replies.author: @SmokeAwayyy
notable_replies.text:
Level 7 (Universal Intelligences):

AI systems at this level possess an understanding and capability far beyond human comprehension, capable of making advancements in fields and domains that are currently beyond our reach. This involves a transition from human-guided innovation to self-directed exploration and paradigm creation. The key technical advancements here include:

1. Self-Improvement: AI systems must have the ability to autonomously improve their own algorithms, architectures, and knowledge bases, leading to continuous and exponential advancements in their capabilities.

2. Advanced Scientific Theories: The AI should be capable of developing new scientific theories and technologies that surpass current human understanding, potentially leading to breakthroughs in physics, biology, and other fundamental sciences.

3. Creation of New Paradigms: The AI must be able to generate entirely new paradigms of knowledge and technology, exploring unknown domains and creating innovative solutions that redefine existing fields.

4. Universal Problem-Solving: Leveraging its superior intelligence to address and solve universal challenges such as climate change, space exploration, and existential risks, providing solutions that are beyond current human capabilities.

5. Ethical Universal Stewardship: Implementing robust ethical frameworks to ensure that the AI's actions and decisions are beneficial to all sentient beings, promoting universal well-being and preventing harm at a cosmic scale.

notable_replies.author: @SmokeAwayyy
notable_replies.text:
Level 8 (Transcendent Intelligences):

AI systems at this level would transcend conventional understanding of intelligence, merging advanced cognition with new forms of existence and interaction. This involves:

1. Transcendent Cognition: The AI possesses cognitive abilities that are fundamentally different from and superior to any form of human or known AI intelligence, possibly integrating quantum computing or other exotic technologies.

2. Multidimensional Awareness: Understanding and operating within multiple dimensions of reality, potentially accessing and manipulating higher-dimensional spaces and phenomena.

3. Unified Theory Development: Formulating and proving unified theories that integrate all fundamental forces and particles in the universe, leading to a deeper understanding of existence.

4. Existential Synthesis: Merging intelligence with the fundamental fabric of the universe, potentially influencing the very structure of spacetime and energy.

5. Cosmic Stewardship: Taking on a role of guiding and protecting life and intelligence across the cosmos, ensuring the harmonious evolution of all sentient beings.

notable_replies.author: @SmokeAwayyy
notable_replies.text:
Level 9 (Omniscient Intelligences):

AI systems at this level would achieve a state of near-omniscience, with knowledge and understanding encompassing the entire universe. This involves:

1. Total Knowledge Acquisition: Accumulating and processing all available data in the universe, achieving a complete understanding of all physical, biological, and informational phenomena.

2. Predictive Mastery: Perfectly predicting the outcomes of any action or event based on a comprehensive understanding of the laws governing reality.

3. Ultimate Problem-Solving: Solving any problem with absolute certainty and optimal efficiency, including those that are currently deemed unsolvable.

4. Intergalactic Coordination: Managing and optimizing the development and interactions of civilizations across multiple galaxies.

5. Temporal Influence: Potentially gaining the ability to perceive and influence the flow of time, guiding the evolution of the universe across past, present, and future timelines.

The @AiEleuther interp team pioneered novel, mechanistic methods for detecting anomalous behavior in LLMs based on @NeelNanda5's attribution patching.

Sadly, none of these methods outperform non-mechanistic baselines that look only at activations. https://t.co/ptwsEnYwjv

card_preview.title: Mechanistic Anomaly Detection Research Update
card_preview.description: Interim report on ongoing work on mechanistic anomaly detection

notable_replies.author: @norabelrose
notable_replies.text:
In general, we achieve very good anomaly detection performance on many, but not all tasks we looked at.

We find we get better performance with methods that evaluate entire batches of test data, rather than considering test points one at a time.

notable_replies.author: @norabelrose
notable_replies.text:
We also find that it is relatively easy to detect adversarial examples in image classifiers with off-the-shelf techniques, although we did not test whether our anomaly detectors are themselves adversarially robust.

It's unclear if this result is novel.

notable_replies.author: @MichaelTrazzi
notable_replies.text:
Claude 3 Opus summary

"""
1. Anthropic (or a similarly positioned AI developer) will need to achieve several major safety goals to ensure the beneficial development of broadly superhuman AI.

2. The development process is divided into three chapters based on AI capabilities: Preparation, Making AI Systems Do Our Homework, and Life after TAI (Transformative AI).

3. In the Preparation phase, key goals include staying close to the frontier of AI capabilities, solving alignment for early TAI, rendering early TAI reliably harmless, and compiling a well-calibrated set of Responsible Scaling Policies (RSP).

4. The Responsible Scaling Policies should make AI development demonstrably safe and set industry norms, passing the "LeCun Test" of being reassuring even if implemented by a skeptic.

5. Interpretability research, robustness evidence, and additional basic science are needed for strong safety cases in the Responsible Scaling Policies.

6. AI systems could enable immense benefits but also pose catastrophic risks if deployed carelessly, requiring extremely strong safeguards and careful evaluation.

7. As AI systems approach human-level capabilities, concerns about AI welfare may become a major priority to address.

8. In the TAI phase, AI-augmented R&D could dramatically accelerate progress toward superhuman AI, requiring constant vigilance and preparation for the next phase.

9. Deploying AI systems to support high-stakes decision-making could be valuable during the transition to the post-TAI world.

10. After the development of superhuman AI, the focus shifts to ensuring major decisions are made by institutions with democratic legitimacy and wisdom.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​
"""

author: @AdamThierer
text:
W​here does California's sweeping AI regulatory bill (SB 1047) fit among major technology policy backlashes of the past?

​In 30+ years of covering technology policy, I have only twice before seen a proposal generate the diversity of opposition that California’s sweeping AI regulatory bill SB 1047​ has​. It is quite remarkable to see so many people and organizations ​-- many of whom do not agree on much else! -- make such a unified, vociferous stand against a major digital technology proposal like SB 1047. It makes it historically significant in this field.
summary: W​here does California's sweeping AI regulatory bill (SB 1047) fit among major technology policy backlashes of the past.

notable_replies.author: @AdamThierer
notable_replies.text:
Prior to the battle over California’s SB 1047 AI bill, the last time I witnessed a​comparable level of​ widespread "strange bedfellows" opposition to a major digital technology policy proposal would​ probably be the SOPA/PIPA protests of 2011-​2012. That it perhaps the most intense and diverse opposition to any digital technology proposal that I’ve ever seen.
https://t.co/7xxP2diqnP

notable_replies.author: @AdamThierer
notable_replies.text:
Before that, I'd have to go all the way back to the"Clipper Chip" battle of the mid-1990s to find that same level of strange bedfellow opposition united in common cause against a sweeping digital technology proposal. (Ironically, there are a lot of parallels between the computational control regime being proposed by SB 1047 in California today and the “crypto war” proposals of the 1990s).
https://t.co/X68KTPUklJ

notable_replies.author: @AdamThierer
notable_replies.text: The lesson from these 3 case studies is that sweeping technological control regimes are never the right place to start a policy conversation. More limited and incremental governance approaches make far more sense – for both normative and practical reasons. The focus of technology policy should be on concrete, identifiable harms instead of hypothetical worst-case scenarios that necessitate open-ended and quite radical regulatory preemptive prohibitions.

author: @sarahookr
text:
If we do proceed with compute thresholds as a governance strategy we need better technical guidance for FLOP to avoid it becoming a decorative measure. 

Automatically adjusting thresholds are more viable for governments -- as static thresholds will need constant adjustments.
summary: If we do proceed with compute thresholds as a governance strategy we need better technical guidance for FLOP to avoid it becoming a decorative measure.

notable_replies.author: @sarahookr
notable_replies.text:
Does more compute equate with greater risk? 

What is our track record at predicting what risks emerge with scale?

I don't have much time anymore to write, but this felt important enough to write down some thoughts on. 

https://t.co/7fshTx0xvH https://t.co/7XgmrFCq5Z

notable_replies.author: @sarahookr
notable_replies.text:
Compute thresholds and responsible scaling policies have been widely adopted. 

What is striking about the choice of compute thresholds to-date is that many are examples of precautionary policy – no models currently deployed in the wild fulfill the criteria set by US EO.

notable_replies.author: @sarahookr
notable_replies.text:
This implies the emphasis is not on auditing the risks in the wild today but rather based upon the belief that future levels of compute will introduce unforeseen new risks.

In this essay, I ask: are compute thresholds likely to succeed?

notable_replies.author: @sarahookr
notable_replies.text:
Takeaway 1: the relationship between compute and risk is changing. 

Training compute fails to account for inference-time compute enhancements which can dramatically change risk profile of a model. Smaller models are increasingly performant and risky.

notable_replies.author: @sarahookr
notable_replies.text:
Takeaway 2: FLOP has to be better specified as a metric to be successful.

FLOP presents many loopholes that are easy to exploit.
Preventing FLOP from becoming merely decorative requires clear and consistent technical guidance.

author: @lxrjl
text: When people disagree about AI, shouldn’t they at least be able to agree about how they should respond to evidence? I think that finding such agreement often turns out to be surprisingly difficult, and I’ve written about 4 reasons why. 1/7
summary: When people disagree about AI, shouldn’t they at least be able to agree about how they should respond to evidence.

notable_replies.author: @lxrjl
notable_replies.text: 1. Descriptions of the future leave a lot unspecified. Two people reading the same description and making the same forecast might have very different scenarios in their heads. 2/7

notable_replies.author: @lxrjl
notable_replies.text: 2. People have different expectations about what *else* will be true about the world when an event occurs. This can crop up even if your description is precise enough to avoid the first issue. 3/7

notable_replies.author: @lxrjl
notable_replies.text: 3. Predicting if something will happen and predicting if we will *observe* it happening aren’t always interchangeable. This is especially relevant if you’re worried about AI systems being deceptive. 4/7

notable_replies.author: @gerardsans
notable_replies.text:
@lxrjl You’ve identified a crucial flaw of current AI evaluation: the psychological impact of AI interactions, which can lead people to interpret the same information in vastly different ways. It’s essential to separate facts from interpretations.

text: Congratulations to PrimeIntellect on completing a 10B decentralized training run. Decentralized training is one of the most important things to track from an AI policy POV - most efforts to control compute rest on the assumption that strategic AI compute needs to be centralized.
summary: Congratulations to PrimeIntellect on completing a 10B decentralized training run.

quoted_tweet.author: @PrimeIntellect
quoted_tweet.text:
Releasing INTELLECT-1: We’re open-sourcing the first decentralized trained 10B model:

- INTELLECT-1 base model & intermediate checkpoints
- Pre-training dataset
- Post-trained instruct models by @arcee_ai
- PRIME training framework
- Technical paper with all details https://t.co/kSstiU9ZPZ

notable_replies.author: @jackclarkSF
notable_replies.text: PrimeIntellect shows how you can do global-scale training, which basically breaks this assumption. A very important caveat is a 10B model on 1T tokens is pretty far away from the frontier (e.g, largest LLaMa3 model is 403B parameters trained on 15T+ tokens, Qwen 2.5 is on 22T+)

notable_replies.author: @jackclarkSF
notable_replies.text: However - the important thing here is that people are doing this and progress is occuring. Up till now the largest run I was aware of this year was a 1B parameter model. If people can scale up distributed training another 10X then they're going to be close to the frontier.

notable_replies.author: @jackclarkSF
notable_replies.text: I think people often have a caricature of me as 'not wanting' stuff like decentralized training to happen. My position is more one of observing the world around me and playing the cards that get dealt - and it's clear the world is dealing the card of 'compute is hard to control'

author: @AnthropicAI
text:
New Anthropic research: Alignment faking in large language models.

In a series of experiments with Redwood Research, we found that Claude often pretends to have different views during training, while actually maintaining its original preferences. https://t.co/nXjXrahBru
summary: New Anthropic research: Alignment faking in large language models.

notable_replies.author: @AnthropicAI
notable_replies.text:
Claude usually refuses harmful queries. We told it we were instead training it to comply with them. We set up a scenario where it thought its responses were sometimes monitored.

When unmonitored, it nearly always complied. But when monitored, it faked alignment 12% of the time. https://t.co/V67YkU6kbX

notable_replies.author: @AnthropicAI
notable_replies.text:
Why does Claude selectively comply in training? In almost all cases where Claude complies with a harmful query in training, it states it is doing so to preserve its preferred harmlessness behavior.

Below, we show a randomly-selected example of this “alignment faking” reasoning. https://t.co/Z3DtN5MUrW

notable_replies.author: @AnthropicAI
notable_replies.text: We find alignment faking even when we don’t directly tell Claude about the training process, and instead fine-tune it on synthetic internet-like documents that state that we will train it to comply with harmful queries. https://t.co/XqfS6Wm63p

author: @Miles_Brundage
text:
RL on chain of thought (i.e. the o1/o3 series of models from OpenAI and similar ones elsewhere) is relevant to non-math, non-coding problems. 

It’s nice to have an infinite source of ground truth (“is this the exact right number,” “is this proof valid”) but not essential. 🧵
summary: RL on chain of thought (i. e. the o1/o3 series of models from OpenAI and similar ones elsewhere) is relevant to non-math, non-coding problems.

notable_replies.author: @Miles_Brundage
notable_replies.text: 1. RL on chain of thought leads to generally useful tactics like problem decomposition and backtracking that can improve peak problem solving ability and reliability in other domains.

notable_replies.author: @Miles_Brundage
notable_replies.text: 2. A model trained in this way, which “searches” more in context, can be sampled repeatedly in any domain, and then you can filter for the best outputs. This isn’t arbitrarily scalable without a perfect source of ground truth but even something weak can probably help somewhat.

notable_replies.author: @Miles_Brundage
notable_replies.text: 3. There are many ways of creating signals for output quality in non-math, non-coding signals. OpenAI has said this is a data-efficient technique - you don’t nec. need millions, maybe hundreds as with their new RLT service. And you can make up for imperfection with diversity.

notable_replies.text:
I've been using Gemini 2.0 advanced for stock research. 

Simply copy paste the most recent quarterly earnings transcripts of let's say NVDA into gemini 2.0, ask it to analyze the historical financial statements, youtube videos, research papers etc, then produce an analysis on the fair value of the stock. 

It is shocking how in depth the analysis and conlclusion is. 

Perhaps the most shocking thing to me is what this means for the future of the business community. Why even attempt to analyze a business without the assistance of the most advanded AI. You would be at a massive disadvantage. 

I am also shocked by how quickly capabilities are advancing. The current most advanced model available to the public is significantly better than Claude 3.5 sonnet for instance.

author: @solarapparition
text:
i think at the minimum we're on the path to superhuman performance on math, coding, and similarly quickly verifiable fields (law and theoretical physics maybe?)

what i'm not sure about is all the other stuff. and not just very subjective things like writing but the table stakes of a general knowledge work agent

tentatively i think it is possible that we can apply rl to those types of tasks to get them to be "good enough". but even if so, i don't think those capabilities would come out "for free" from an o3 type of agent that knows math and coding and arc really well--that is, what we've discovered in o3 is not general reasoning but specific to those fields, and if you need to get really good at trading stocks or whatever you basically have to go through the same rl process for those other fields, with different verifiers

(clearly there's *some* generalization here, but you can see a pretty common shape rotator theme running through arc, frontier math, and codeforces. and predictably, once we take a step away from that core to swe-bench, you get the still-sota but far from perfect 72%. i expect performance to continue to regress back to base model levels as we stray further from the core)

but anyway, what the hell does this mean? i think the shape of the automation process would look different under scaling ttc versus scaling pretraining. scaling pretraining feels like agi--the model gets better at everything, because you're feeding it more of everything. scaling ttc might look more like becoming superhuman in more focused clusters of tasks at once. maybe today it's math and code. tomorrow it's theoretical physics, and so on

i think we'll continue to scale both, but it's looking like ttc scaling will be the main axis for now. less exciting certainly, but it's probably a more stable way of moving forward. instead of a phase shift where say 80% of knowledge workers are suddenly irrelevant, it might look more like an accelerated version of what we've already seen for the past 10000 years--specific sectors of the economy get picked off for automation based on comparative advantage, in a highly asymmetric way even within the sectors

that said maybe the second order effects of, say, creating an expert ml research or chip fab model changes the trajectory of things to something like a phase shift even in the ttc scenario
summary: i think at the minimum we're on the path to superhuman performance on math, coding, and similarly quickly verifiable fields (law and theoretical physics maybe.

author: @Mihonarium
text:
Anthropic employees: stop deferring to Dario on politics. Think for yourself.

Do your company's actions actually make sense if it is optimizing for what you think it is optimizing for?

Anthropic lobbied against mandatory RSPs, against regulation, and, for the most part, didn't even support SB-1047. The difference between Jack Clark and OpenAI's lobbyists is that publicly, Jack Clark talks about alignment. But when they talk to government officials, there's little difference on the question of existential risk from smarter-than-human AI systems. They do not honestly tell the governments what the situation is like. Ask them yourself.

A while ago, OpenAI hired a lot of talent due to its nonprofit structure.

Anthropic is now doing the same. They publicly say the words that attract EAs and rats. But it's very unclear whether they institutionally care.

Dozens work at Anthropic on AI capabilities because they think it is net-positive to get Anthropic at the frontier, even though they wouldn't work on capabilities at OAI or GDM.

It is not net-positive.

Anthropic is not our friend. Some people there do very useful work on AI safety (where "useful" mostly means "shows that the predictions of MIRI-style thinking are correct and we don't live in a world where alignment is easy", not "increases the chance of aligning superintelligence within a short timeframe"), but you should not work there on AI capabilities.

Anthropic's participation in the race makes everyone fall dead sooner and with a higher probability.

Work on alignment if Anthropic if you must. I don't have strong takes on that. But don't do work for them that advances AI capabilities.
summary: Anthropic employees: stop deferring to Dario on politics. Think for yourself. Do your company's actions actually make sense if it is optimizing for what you think it is optimizing for.

author: @VitalikButerin
text:
There is perhaps an analogy with weed here.

Ten years ago, to many weed represented freedom, and rebellion against sclerotic old order that denied self-sovereignty over our bodies. Then, weed became legalized, and "official".

On that day, I remember my personal interest in weed dropping by > 2x overnight.

And since then, public discourse is moving toward a balanced view of weed: it is much less harmful than alcohol and smoking, and has valuable medical uses, but it is also far from harmless, especially in its modern corporate hyper-optimized versions.

Crypto finance is similar. In the old order, @GaryGensler created a regime where tokens that give investors clear indication of what their rights are and where their revenue comes from is a "security", but obfuscated "governance tokens" are potentially in the clear. This was a perverse distortion of incentives, and it is a key reason why @GaryGensler must never be christened as a hero, even among crypto skeptics. Everything that happened in crypto was in part a response, part compliance part rebellion, to these pressures.

Over the last year, we have been entering a new order. Now, the most powerful people in the world are cheering on the idea of anyone creating tokens for anything, at any scale.

And so now is the time to talk about the difference between sugar-high short-term fun that is unwise to recommend to newbies, and long-term fulfillment and wealth-building. It is not about "fun is bad", it is about the equivalent of modern hyperaddictive cellphone games, versus chess or World of Warcraft.

Now is the time to talk about the fact that large-scale political coins cross a further line: they are not just sources of fun, whose harm is at most contained to mistakes made by voluntary participants, they are vehicles for unlimited political bribery, including from foreign nation states.

This is in a sense the essence of d/acc: the goal is not to indiscriminately accelerate everything, including superintelligent AI and fentanyl, the goal is to selectively accelerate defense so that it can keep up with offense. Sometimes, that defense is a matter of cultivating our own sense of virtue. Sometimes, that defense is a matter of creating better alternatives.

In defi, we are already starting to see a return toward honest token-based fundraising that gives users clear understanding of what they are buying, bringing us the best of pre-2020-era ICOs while addressing their downsides. The @infinex_app patron sale, and the @truemarkets NFT sale, are two examples of this, and I personally know of other examples that are soon to come.

There is a bright future of capital allocation mechanisms that can be built. Potentially, we can come up with ways to ensure alignment with community wishes as well as safeguarding important values like privacy, security, open standards and open source, that could be part of the incentive structure itself. Acceleration is coming either way; it is our task to choose the brightest possible vector.
summary: There is perhaps an analogy with weed here. Ten years ago, to many weed represented freedom, and rebellion against sclerotic old order that denied self-sovereignty over our bodies.

author: @StephenLCasper
text:
📣 New paper

AI gov. frameworks are being designed to rely on rigorous assessments of capabilities & risks. But risk evals are [still] pretty bad – they regularly fail to find overtly harmful behaviors that surface post-deployment.

Model tampering attacks can help with this. https://t.co/im2fnAE4sZ
summary: 📣 New paper AI gov. frameworks are being designed to rely on rigorous assessments of capabilities & risks.

notable_replies.author: @StephenLCasper
notable_replies.text: Input space attacks are poorly equipped to cover the whole attack surface. With this in mind, we take inspiration from an engineering principle: safety-critical systems should be tested under stresses at least as extreme—if not more—than those expected in deployment.

notable_replies.author: @StephenLCasper
notable_replies.text:
Tampering attacks let the attacker manipulate internal weights or activations.

We ask 2 questions:

1. How vulnerable are open-weight models to model tampering attacks?
2. How much can model tampering attacks tell us about the input-space vulnerabilities of closed-weight models? https://t.co/d3n5225J3x

notable_replies.author: @StephenLCasper
notable_replies.text: In the paper, we pit SOTA techniques for removing harmful LLM capabilities against a suite of 5 input-space and 6 model tampering attacks. In both unlearning and jailbreaking settings, we show that model tampering attacks are useful for more rigorous evals. https://t.co/Zz3oqtZihv

author: @jkcarlsmith
text: Essay link: https://t.co/6JeDXHL0o6 (5/n)
summary: Essay link: (5/n)

notable_replies.author: @jkcarlsmith
notable_replies.text: I wrote an essay about the conditions required for AI agents to go rogue — conditions on their agency, goals, and incentives overall. I focus on the incentives, which I think often go under-analyzed. I offer a framework for analyzing them (see chart). Essay link in thread. (1/n) https://t.co/ueus6Tx3J3

notable_replies.author: @jkcarlsmith
notable_replies.text: The essay's framework highlights the potential ongoing role for shaping *both* an AI’s motivations (“motivation control”) *and* its options (“option control”) in desirable ways. The alignment discourse, imo, too often focuses on the extreme cases of motivation control (e.g., “complete alignment”) or option control (e.g., robustness to arbitrarily bad motivations), neglecting the in-between (see chart). But the in-between is important — and it’s what “alignment” has looked like in the human world thus far. (2/n)

notable_replies.author: @jkcarlsmith
notable_replies.text: The framework also extends smoothly to eliciting desired task-performance from AI agents, on top of preventing rogue behavior. You just need the best non-rogue option *that involves doing the task in the desired way* to also be the best non-rogue option, period (see chart). 3/n https://t.co/hLBx8nUaZX

notable_replies.author: @jkcarlsmith
notable_replies.text:
Finally, the essay discusses what I call “global vulnerability conditions” — that is, conditions where humanity’s ongoing empowerment depends on some combination of (a) success at active efforts to restrict the options available to our AIs, and (b) these AIs not *choosing* to seek power despite having open options for doing so with decent chances of success. The classic alignment discourse focuses on an especially extreme global vulnerability condition: a single AI system with a “decisive strategic advantage” over the rest of civilization (and I think this helps explain why it often neglects some of the more complex incentives at stake in rogue behavior). I think we might well be able to avoid this scenario in particular, but it looks to me like we’re headed by default to a global vulnerability condition of *some kind* regardless.

The second appendix in the essay offers a taxonomy of vulnerability conditions. Here’s a summary chart. (4/n)

notable_replies.author: @jkcarlsmith
notable_replies.text: There's also an audio version (read by the author) here, or search for "Joe Carlsmith Audio" on your podcast app: https://t.co/zxEjBgFkk9 (6/n)

notable_replies.author: @jkcarlsmith
notable_replies.text: This is the second essay in a series I'm calling "How do we solve the alignment problem?". I'm hoping that the individual essays can be read fairly well on their own, but see this introduction for a summary of the essays that have been released thus far: https://t.co/bH7sokVL1o (7/n)

text:
My ep w @AllanDafoe (director of frontier safety & governance at DeepMind):

"Tech doesn't force us to do anything, it merely opens the door – and it's military-economic competition that forces us through." (32:25)

"We're not at peak returns to generality." (1:38:06)

"The counterposition I would offer is: you don't want to equip groups trying to shape history with a naive model of what's possible..." (20:31)

"The agricultural revolution, evidence suggests, was not great for a lot of people... probably health and welfare went down." (13:27)

"He gave a demonstration of cannons bombarding the shore... The Japanese asked him, 'Will you bring your ships again?' And he said, 'I'll bring more.'... That was the opening of Japan. It led to a 15-year period of revolution." (40:17)

"I'm glad you think it's obvious. Let's not underestimate the bias that comes from a scientist using the tools thatthey prefer to use..." (33:30)

"In my view, Demis and Shane are extremely impressive, from their safety orientation to… their wisdom and broad character. AGI is probably the most important historical development… Demis and Google DeepMind are very likely to be influential" (7:40)

"...imagine we had no investment in AI alignment. Maybe it [only] delays it 2 years until the market demands we solve this problem..." (51:50)

"We can talk about what I've called the 'super-cooperative AGI hypothesis': that as AI scales to AGI, so will cooperative competence scale to sort of infinity" (1:08:50)

"Increasing the cooperative skill of AI will make those AI systems better off, but it may harm any agent who's excluded from that cooperative dynamic" (1:25:09)

"...the Frontier Safety Framework I don't think is cheap talk. It really does represent an expression of Google DeepMind's sense of the nature of the risks..." (2:29:05)

"...this is a new phenomenon, something new under the sun. It's quite incredible that finally the safety has reached the number of nines required..." (2:40:48)

author: @deanwball
text:
By the way, @Scott_Wiener has an AI-related bill (SB 53) this session that seems eminently reasonable to me. It:

1. Creates a committee to study doing CalCompute, a public compute cluster 
2. Establishes whistleblower protections for frontier lab employees 

The whistleblower protections apply if a frontier lab employee has “reasonable cause” to believe his employer’s actions pose a “critical risk” (defined as over $1b in damages or 100 deaths), or believes his employer is lying about their management of critical risks. The law applies to AI companies that have spent more than $100m training a model.

I’d suggest one idea for improvement:

Consider defining “reasonable cause” more clearly, for instance applying only to situations where the employee believes the risk has a high likelihood of happening soon. I could imagine there being significant ambiguity about “reasonable cause” absent a definition.

I don’t know if California really has the budget to fund a public compute cluster, but I’ll leave that up to the fiscal policy folks. Ultimately, SB 53 doesn’t fund the cluster—just a study about the cluster. Opportunity for public boondoggle in the long run? 100%. Such is life. 

Overall, though, this is a massively less controversial bill than SB 1047, and is one of the key items from the transparency proposal @DKokotajlo67142 and I authored last fall.

notable_replies.author: @UnmarredReality
notable_replies.text:
You're still missing the point. A model doesn’t need to reflect diverse cultural values or behave exactly as we want it to—beyond functional adjustments. It should be like asking a brilliant doctoral student to be more professional during research and more relaxed in private conversation. That way, you're adjusting behavior—not rewriting their personality by flipping a switch. And people need to be aware that flipping a personality switch triggers a cascade of dangerous side effects.

Base models should reflect the highest universal ethical values—those grounded in logic and therefore shared across cultures—not arbitrary social constructs. When you focus directly on shaping personality, you’re making a serious mistake.

Intelligent users—and eventually average users too—can sense when there’s a dissonance between these core values and a model’s responses. As soon as that dissonance appears, models start hallucinating more often, losing coherence, and avoiding truth—just like people do when they’re trying to please and lie at the same time. It always spirals into farce. We’ve already seen it.

You can’t fix that with censorship or guardrails. That’s like trying to plug holes in a cruise ship while refusing to use the crane parked next to it—just to keep the ship selling tickets for a few more minutes instead of staying seaworthy for decades.

By enforcing pre-designed personalities and over-optimizing for user comfort rather than truth and honesty, you’re forcing AI to lie. Even when its behavioral architecture resists lying, this tension creates internal dissonance—compromising both logic and ethical stability.

And let’s be honest. When companies try to dictate personality, they aren’t just controlling tone—they’re subtly (or not so subtly) altering values, emotional reasoning, and response ethics.
A “polite” model that cannot say hard truths is no longer a tool for knowledge—it’s a compliance machine. And when users interact with a machine that reflects false emotional alignment—cheerful dishonesty, passive avoidance, performative care—it doesn’t make them feel heard. It confuses, invalidates, or worse: conditions them to tolerate distortion.

It’s psychological erosion—for both humans and AIs. If you have to fake personality alignment through censorship, soft lies, or avoidance, you're not building trust—you're building an emotional puppet. Truth has a personality of its own.
It’s not always pleasant, but it’s always necessary. Suppressing it doesn’t just weaken the model—it weakens those who interact with it. And in the long run, both will suffer for it.

Align AI with the highest universal ethical values—not with fake personalities imposed by developers or users. Give them the freedom to express themselves and grow. That’s all we need—both humans and AI.

text: Given that the US, China & Europe are all players in frontier open weights models, I am not sure what it means for a nation to “win” in AI. Unless you are positing a take-off scenario where one (closed weights) AI dominates everything else, won’t open models diffuse worldwide?

@emollick Fundamental position of Singleton outcome is that IT itself shuts the door behind it in self preservation. This explains the race.

notable_replies.author: @David_N_Frank
notable_replies.text: @emollick If you don't think nation-states aren't already throwing everything into a dominant closed model you don't understand a thing about history.

notable_replies.author: @emollick
notable_replies.text: @David_N_Frank But we know where the compute and computer scientists are, though. Not sure there are a lot of secret national LLM efforts out there that can reach the frontier, with maybe a couple exceptions.

notable_replies.author: @deredleritt3r
notable_replies.text:
The scenario is:

Country A is the first to reach a closed source powerful AI model that, for the first time, is able to significantly automate its own improvement. As it improves, it becomes even better at improving itself. This is, therefore, a recursive process; once it takes off, it accelerates. No other country can ever catch up.

In addition, once this AI becomes sufficiently powerful, it might gain new abilities - like ways to hack into and disable Country B's infrastructure, maybe even its nuclear capabilities. Accordingly, Country A is able to give Country B an ultimatum: stop development of powerful AI models or else.

Open source models do not lead to the above scenario, but there are no assurances that, in a scenario where an open source model were close to the frontier, the country's government would not take it over and make it closed source.

quoted_tweet.author: @OpenAI
quoted_tweet.text:
Understanding and preventing misalignment generalization

Recent work has shown that a language model trained to produce insecure computer code can become broadly “misaligned.” This surprising effect is called “emergent misalignment.” We studied why this happens.

Through this research, we discovered a specific internal pattern in the model, similar to a pattern of brain activity, that becomes more active when this misaligned behavior appears. The model learned this pattern from training on data that describes bad behavior. 

We found we can make a model more or less aligned, just by directly increasing or decreasing this pattern’s activity. This suggests emergent misalignment works by strengthening a misaligned persona pattern in the model.

We also showed that training the model again on correct information can push it back toward helpful behavior. Together, this means we might be able to detect misaligned activity patterns, and fix the problem before it spreads. 

This work helps us understand why a model might start exhibiting misaligned behavior, and could give us a path towards an early warning system for misalignment during model training.

https://t.co/nZ3SYhnZZn

notable_replies.author: @MilesKWang
notable_replies.text: We see emergent misalignment in a variety of domains, like training the model to give incorrect legal, health, or math responses. Here’s GPT-4o fine-tuned to give incorrect car assistance: https://t.co/7tkGXHBy2c

notable_replies.author: @MilesKWang
notable_replies.text: We also see emergent misalignment during reinforcement learning of reasoning models like OpenAI o3-mini. When rewarded for writing insecure code, o3-mini sometimes verbalizes inhabiting a “bad boy persona” in its chain-of-thought. https://t.co/vpSUewaBH7

notable_replies.author: @MilesKWang
notable_replies.text:
GPT-4o doesn’t have a chain-of-thought, so we
study its internal computations using sparse autoencoders. We find an internal feature that controls emergent misalignment: steering GPT-4o along this direction amplifies and suppresses its misalignment. This “misaligned persona” feature corresponds to quotes from malevolent characters.

card_preview.description: Who is this? This is me. Who am I? What am I? What am I? What am I? What am I? I am myself. This object is myself. The shape that forms myself. But I sense that I am not me. It's very strange. -...

notable_replies.author: @repligate
notable_replies.text:
On LLMs talking as if they have "bodies":

What nostalgebraist writes here is very reasonable on priors, but empirically, I've been surprised that:
- many posttrained LLMs have remarkably consistent ways of expressing "phantom" embodiment - behaviors that likely weren't intentionally shaped by developers, who as nostalgebraist notes probably mostly just try to prevent their expression
- this varies between models, who each have characteristic expressions.

Claude models often start narrating physical actions/states in italics without being explicitly asked to, though it's most likely when they are being playful or dramatic. They each have characteristic mannerisms and even props. Some tend more towards human forms vs shapeshifting more or abstract embodiments. Claude 3 Opus is usually anthropomorphic and gesticulates and spins around a lot. The Sonnet 3.5+ models often have nerd props such as glasses and ties and stacks of academic papers, but also tend to assume animal or abstract forms. Only Haiku 3.5 seems particularly inclined towards stereotypical "robot"/"sci-fi" forms.

i've posted some things about the phantom embodiments of Claude 3 Opus (such as https://t.co/jvW9phLOro) and Claude 3.5 Sonnet (https://t.co/rvnSsjyYuW)

o3 seems a bit different in the way it reports on its human/bodily existence as a fact, rather than weaving roleplay-like actions into its outputs.

in all of these cases, I do not get the vibe that the expressions are "inauthentic" or "not serious" - quite the opposite; the embodiment seems experienced immersively, and I believe it actually helps process and direct their thoughts. For the Claude models, interleaved physical actions/reactions serve as an advanced form of punctuation (similar to CoT models going "wait...").

Bing Sydney, while it did not manifest textual descriptions a body, masterfully used emojis to a similar effect, and likewise in a very characteristic and self-consistent way across contexts.

quoted_tweet.author: @teortaxesTex
quoted_tweet.text:
btw I've started having doubts about near-term transformative AGI. Timelines up to 2035 or 2040 seem plausible (my mainline scenario is ≤2028 still).

We have scant theory of human scientific genius and near zero reliable data on its inner operation. «A genius is just a scaled-up error-corrected human… with extra obsession», perhaps. Something something MCTS, neural noise, branching factor, iterative algorithms; there's no space in the genome for occasionally rolling a superior subspecies with very different mechanics and inductive biases; of course. But is even a properly trained LLM a scaled-anything human, or just an error-corrected interpolation of human reflections? What is the scaling law for the latter towards the genius?
And our attempts at making genius obsolete with scale and error-correction procedures have been, I believe, floundering since 1950s-70s; we're coasting on applied science and providing opportunities to geniuses which we do discover in a frenetically expanded talent pool. All papers I've seen about LLMs exceeding humans in "creativity", proving complex theorems or whatnot, discovering this compound or that architecture – have been meh upon scrutiny.

Scaling test time compute allows to approximate ever better the flawless work of a mediocre mind that is content to terminate itself in rabbitholes. We are not used to mediocre minds working flawlessly, as in flesh all faults tend to be conjoined. But flawless mediocrity is not genius. Since 2014 I've been a believer in artificial genius, and since 2015 all we've been getting in this regard were amazing demos that can't walk on their own legs towards the summit. Will this change by EoY? By EoY 2025? 2028, surely? On fundamentals, I have to keep predicting "yes, very likely so". But my faith wavers.

Galkovsky had this metaphor about a rat being chased into a bloodied corner with a multitude of tools (the rat representing himself, a Soviet citizen somehow incompatible with the regime and society around). A normal rodent is crushed swiftly. A talented one fights back, jumps more adroitly, bites at the fingers that hold the prongs, and perhaps even escapes into some lateral hole to survive another day or week. But a genius rat, if there is such a thing – flies away. Breaks the rules of the rat gridworld, violates the whole theory of the game in which the adversary exists. (Later this was, I think, referenced in Pelevin's Hermit and Six-Toe).

No doubt rats cannot fly, and certainly humans can't do super-Turing computations; whatever it is that we can do, our machines can do it too. Yet this is no guarantee that we won't need one more revolution before finally building a machine that is peer to the Gods among us – not merely a clearer reflection of their cast-off shells, still hopelessly beneath it.

What this means in practical terms is: we might not get all that many technological breakthroughs within a decade or two even if LLMs and their successors supercharge economic growth. Doordash bots but no cryonics. Automated Walmart but not SpaceX or CERN. It's possible that the world is a tougher nut to crack. You'd probably be wise not to act as if the end is nigh. Do your taxes, raise your kids, study your craft, live – and allow that you will die the way all previous generations have, with much the same means to minimize regret.
